two-sum.question: What if each number could ask for its missing partner?
intuition: Imagine four number tiles and a target total of nine. We need two different tiles that fill that total exactly. Trying every pair works, but each new tile makes us revisit the earlier tiles one by one. The question becomes much simpler when we turn it around: if this tile is seven, which single value would complete nine?

The missing partner is two. Keep a small address book of numbers already encountered and their positions. Looking up two now answers the whole pairing question in one operation. This is the useful observation: a search through many possible partners can become a question about one exact value.
two-sum.observation: Ask for the missing partner before remembering the current tile. The address book then contains only different, earlier positions.
approach: Read a number and subtract it from the target to find the missing partner.
Look for that partner among earlier numbers. If it is there, the two remembered positions are the answer.
If it is absent, remember this number and its position, then continue.
two-sum.correctness: Every valid pair has an earlier tile and a later tile. When the later one arrives, the earlier one is already remembered. Their values make the target by construction. Since the current tile has not yet entered the address book, it cannot accidentally pair with itself. This explains both why every valid pair can be found and why a reported pair uses two different positions.
two-sum.cost: Read each tile at most once. Looking up and remembering a value take constant time on average, so doubling the number of tiles roughly doubles the work. The address book may need to remember almost all the tiles. Hashing gives an expected, rather than worst-case, linear time bound.
pitfalls: Two equal values can form a pair only when they occupy two separate positions.
The answer is a pair of positions, not the two number values.
Negative numbers and zero follow exactly the same missing-partner reasoning.
two-sum.artAlt: Two glowing puzzle pieces join into one outline, suggesting a number and its missing partner.
two-sum.artCaption: Think of each number as one piece of a target total. Its missing piece must come from another position; the exact example beside this lesson pairs 2 with 7.

scenes.title: Two tiles, one total
scenes.narration: The numbers are 2, 7, 11, and 15. Find two different positions whose values make 9.
scenes.decision: A tile can contribute once. We are finding positions, not creating new numbers.

scenes.title: Why checking every pair repeats work
scenes.narration: We could compare 2 with 7, then 11, then 15, and repeat such comparisons for every next number.
scenes.decision: Those repeated comparisons are the bottleneck. We want to ask a more focused question.

scenes.title: Turn the question around
scenes.narration: For each number, ask what is missing from 9. For 2, the missing partner is 7.
scenes.decision: Only one value can complete a particular number to the target.

scenes.title: Remember the first tile
scenes.narration: No earlier number is available yet. Remember the value 2 and its position, 0.
scenes.decision: Remembering its position lets us later return the location of the pair.

scenes.title: The next tile finds its partner
scenes.narration: The next value is 7. Its missing partner is 2, already remembered at position 0.
scenes.decision: The stored tile is earlier, so these are two different positions.

scenes.title: The answer emerges
scenes.narration: Positions 0 and 1 hold 2 and 7. Their total is 9, so these positions are the answer.
scenes.decision: The required pair is found. The remaining numbers cannot improve an exact answer.

scenes.title: Why no pair is missed
scenes.narration: In any valid pair, the later tile asks for the earlier tile. The earlier tile is waiting in the address book.
scenes.decision: One forward scan eventually examines the later member of the guaranteed pair.

scenes.title: A useful boundary case
scenes.narration: Separate example: a target of 6 with two tiles both valued 3 is valid. A single tile valued 3 cannot be used twice.
scenes.decision: Check before remembering the current tile to preserve the distinct-position rule.

coin-change.question: Why can taking the biggest coin cost more coins?
intuition: Suppose our coins are worth one, three, and four, and we need six. Taking four first feels sensible, but then we need two more coins worth one: three coins in total. Two coins worth three do better. A good first step is not necessarily part of the best complete answer.

Instead, imagine every amount as a destination on a map. Adding a coin is one move. To find the shortest route to six, ask which coin could be the final move. That move must come from a smaller amount. Once we know the best route to every smaller amount, we can compare all final moves without rebuilding those routes.
coin-change.observation: Try every possible last coin, and keep only the smallest coin count for each amount. An unreachable amount cannot supply a route.
approach: Begin with the fact that amount zero needs no coins.
Solve amounts from small to large. For each amount, try removing one allowed final coin.
Add one coin to the best known answer for the remaining amount, and keep the cheapest valid choice.
If no choice reaches the requested amount, report that it is impossible.
coin-change.correctness: Every nonempty collection of coins has a final coin. Remove that coin and a smaller amount remains. If that smaller part could be made with fewer coins, replacing it would also improve the whole collection. Therefore an optimal answer can always use an optimal answer for its remaining amount. Comparing every possible final coin includes the final coin of an optimal collection, so the cheapest candidate is exact.
coin-change.cost: For every amount from zero to the target, compare every denomination. Work grows with the target amount multiplied by the number of denominations. Remember one best count per amount. This measures the amount itself, not merely the number of digits used to write it.
pitfalls: Largest-coin-first fails for arbitrary denominations, as 4 + 1 + 1 versus 3 + 3 shows.
Amount zero needs zero coins.
Impossible smaller amounts must stay separate from valid coin counts.
coin-change.artAlt: Two routes reach six: four plus one plus one uses three coins, while three plus three uses two.
coin-change.artCaption: Two routes reach six: four plus one plus one uses three coins, while three plus three uses two.

scenes.title: The destination is six
scenes.narration: Our denominations are 1, 3, and 4. Each may be used repeatedly. We want the number of coins to be as small as possible.
scenes.decision: Compare counts of coins, not the value of the largest coin.

scenes.title: The tempting shortcut fails
scenes.narration: Taking 4 first leaves 2, which takes two 1s. That is three coins. Taking 3 and 3 uses only two.
scenes.decision: A local choice based on coin size does not guarantee the smallest total count.

scenes.title: Look at the final move
scenes.narration: A last coin worth 3 must follow a route to amount 3. One more coin extends that route to amount 6.
scenes.decision: A positive coin always refers to a smaller amount, whose best answer can already be known.

scenes.title: Build the smaller answers
scenes.narration: Amounts 0 through 5 have best counts 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, and 2. These answers are reused rather than solved again.
scenes.decision: Different ways to reach the same amount need only compete for its cheapest count.

scenes.title: Compare all routes to six
scenes.narration: A final 1 follows amount 5: three coins total. A final 3 follows amount 3: two coins. A final 4 follows amount 2: three coins.
scenes.decision: Choose the least count among every valid final move.

scenes.title: The winning route
scenes.narration: The minimum is two coins, both worth 3. Their values add to 6.
scenes.decision: The answer counts coins; it is not the amount or a list of chosen denominations.

scenes.title: Why the comparison is complete
scenes.narration: Every way of making 6 ends in a 1, a 3, or a 4. All three possibilities were compared.
scenes.decision: The best smaller answer plus that final coin is at least as good as any more expensive smaller route.

scenes.title: Zero is the starting destination
scenes.narration: Boundary example: amount zero is already reached before taking any coin. Its answer is zero, even when no positive target is reachable.
scenes.decision: A real zero-coin answer provides the base from which all valid routes grow.

reverse-linked-list.question: How do we turn a chain around without losing its far end?
intuition: A linked list is a chain of nodes, each carrying an arrow to the next node. Reversing it means turning those arrows around; the node values and identities stay the same. The difficulty is that turning an arrow backward removes our route to the rest of the chain.

Imagine a bookmark placed at the next untouched node before we turn an arrow. Now we can safely join the current node to the front of the reversed chain and follow the bookmark onward. At every moment there are two parts: a completed reversed chain and an untouched chain. One node moves from the second part to the first at each step.
reverse-linked-list.observation: Bookmark the next untouched node before turning the current arrow backward.
approach: Start with an empty reversed chain and the entire original chain still to visit.
Remember where the current node points before changing its arrow.
Point the current node to the front of the reversed chain. It becomes the new front.
Continue from the bookmarked node. When nothing remains, return the front of the reversed chain.
reverse-linked-list.correctness: Initially every node belongs to the untouched chain. Each move takes exactly its first node and places that same node in front of the reversed chain. The bookmark keeps the remaining nodes reachable, while the reversed part remains correctly linked. No node is copied, lost, or used twice. Once the untouched chain is empty, every original node belongs to the completed reversed chain, whose front is the new starting node.
reverse-linked-list.cost: Each node makes one transfer, so work grows directly with the list length. Only a few bookmarks are needed regardless of how long the chain is. No new output nodes are created.
pitfalls: Save the forward route before reversing a link. Saving it afterward is too late.
Return the new front, which was originally the last node.
Reverse node links rather than simply reversing the stored values.
reverse-linked-list.artAlt: The same nodes form two chains during reversal: a completed 2-to-1 chain and an untouched 3-to-4-to-5 chain. A bookmark preserves the route into the untouched part.
reverse-linked-list.artCaption: The same nodes form two chains during reversal: a completed 2-to-1 chain and an untouched 3-to-4-to-5 chain. A bookmark preserves the route into the untouched part.

scenes.title: A chain of five nodes
scenes.narration: Our list is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. The goal is to follow the same nodes in the opposite order.
scenes.decision: Arrows describe next links. Node identities and values stay fixed.

scenes.title: Why replacing values misses the point
scenes.narration: Copying values in reverse would leave the chain links unchanged. We need to reverse the actual arrows.
scenes.decision: The task is a structural transformation, not merely a different printed sequence.

scenes.title: Keep a route forward
scenes.narration: Before turning a link, bookmark the next untouched node. This preserves access to the rest of the chain.
scenes.decision: The forward arrow is about to disappear, so the bookmark must come first.

scenes.title: Move the first node
scenes.narration: Bookmark node 2. Node 1 now points to the end of the empty reversed part, becoming the final tail.
scenes.decision: The original chain remains reachable from the saved route to node 2.

scenes.title: Grow the reversed chain
scenes.narration: Bookmark node 3, then turn node 2 toward node 1. The completed chain is 2 → 1; the untouched part begins at 3.
scenes.decision: Previously reversed links stay intact as one more node is added at the front.

scenes.title: The last transfer completes it
scenes.narration: Repeat for 3, 4, and 5. The resulting chain is 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. Nothing remains untouched.
scenes.decision: The last original node is now the front of the complete reversed chain.

scenes.title: Why every node survives
scenes.narration: Each transfer preserves the reversed chain and the bookmarked untouched chain. Together they still contain all original nodes.
scenes.decision: Moving one node at a time eventually empties the untouched part without losing any nodes.

scenes.title: When there is no chain
scenes.narration: Boundary example: an empty list has no nodes to move. Its reversed list is also empty.
scenes.decision: The same rule works without a special first-node transfer.

add-two-numbers.question: How does paper addition work when the ones digit comes first?
intuition: A list can represent a number too large for a fixed-size integer. Converting it into one whole number hides the digit-by-digit structure. The lists already put the ones digit first, exactly where paper addition begins.

Treat the lists as aligned addition columns. Each column receives two digits and the carry from the preceding column. Keep its ones digit and send its tens digit to the next column. A finished short list contributes zero to the remaining columns.
add-two-numbers.observation: Finish only when both numbers have no digits left and there is no carry waiting.
approach: Add the next two digits and the incoming carry.
Write the ones digit of that total and carry any remaining ten onward.
Continue until the digits and the final carry are exhausted.
add-two-numbers.correctness: After each column, the written digits equal the low-order digits of the true sum, and the carry accounts for the remaining ten. The next column preserves this equality. Once no digits or carry remain, the written chain represents the entire sum.
add-two-numbers.cost: Visit each input digit once and write at most one extra digit for a final carry. The result needs memory proportional to its digits; beyond those output nodes, only the current columns and carry are remembered.
pitfalls: A shorter number supplies zero in later columns.
The final carry may need another digit.
The output chain begins with the ones digit.
add-two-numbers.artAlt: Aligned digit chains send a carry from one addition column to the next, rather than converting whole numbers.
add-two-numbers.artCaption: Aligned digit chains send a carry from one addition column to the next, rather than converting whole numbers.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.question: How far can a strip of letters grow before a repeat forces it to shrink?
intuition: Checking every possible continuous section repeats the same character comparisons. A section that was valid a moment ago only needs one new question when we add the next letter: does this new letter already appear inside it?

Imagine a movable frame over the string. Extend its far edge one character at a time. When the new character repeats one inside the frame, move the near edge just past that earlier occurrence. Remember the widest valid frame ever seen.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.observation: The start only moves forward. An earlier copy outside the frame does not invalidate the current frame.
approach: Extend the framed section by one character.
If that character already appears inside, move the start just past its previous occurrence.
Remember the greatest valid length after each extension.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.correctness: For each ending position, moving just beyond the latest conflicting character gives the earliest possible valid start. Any earlier start would include a duplicate. Thus the frame is the longest valid section ending there. Taking the maximum over all endings gives the overall longest substring.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.cost: Scan each character once and remember its latest position. The start never moves backward. Time grows with the string length; memory grows with the number of distinct characters encountered.
pitfalls: A substring must be continuous; skipping characters changes the problem.
Do not move the start backward.
Spaces and punctuation count as characters.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.artCaption: A movable frame keeps a continuous strip of unique letters and shifts past the conflicting copy.

median-of-two-sorted-arrays.question: Can we find the middle without merging the sorted rows?
intuition: Merging both rows would reveal the middle, but it reads every value. The median only needs a boundary between the lower half and upper half. Sorted order lets us judge that boundary from just its neighboring values.

Place one cut in each row so the combined lower side holds half the values, rounded up. If both lower-side boundary values are no larger than the opposite upper-side boundary, every lower value belongs before every upper value. Search cut positions in the shorter row.
median-of-two-sorted-arrays.observation: Keep the lower-half size fixed, and make both cross-boundary comparisons hold.
approach: Try a cut in the shorter sorted row and infer the other cut from the required half size.
If one lower boundary is too large, move its cut left; otherwise move it right.
At a valid split, use the largest lower value for an odd total, or average the two middle boundaries for an even total.
median-of-two-sorted-arrays.correctness: Values within each row are already ordered. Only the two cross-row boundaries can violate the split. When both are ordered and the side sizes are correct, every lower value precedes every upper value. These two facts identify the middle exactly. A failed comparison tells which direction the short-row cut must move.
median-of-two-sorted-arrays.cost: Each failed cut discards half the remaining cut positions in the shorter row. Only four boundary values and a few positions are remembered, so extra memory stays constant.
pitfalls: Search cuts in the shorter row.
An odd total uses one middle value; an even total averages two.
A cut at a row edge still has a valid interpretation.

longest-palindromic-substring.question: What happens when we grow a mirror outward from every possible center?
intuition: Trying every substring and checking it in both directions repeats many matching comparisons. A palindrome already has a stronger structure: each new outer pair must match around its center.

A palindrome is like a mirror placed in the middle of a word. Expand outward in matched pairs. The mirror can sit on one character or in a gap between two characters. Try both kinds of center and keep the widest successful expansion.
longest-palindromic-substring.observation: Stop an expansion at the first unequal pair or at the edge of the string.
approach: Choose a character center and a gap center.
Compare outward pairs until they differ or reach an edge.
Keep the longest matching continuous section across all centers.
longest-palindromic-substring.correctness: Every palindrome has either a character center or a gap center. Expanding from that center reproduces all of its matching pairs and may continue to a larger palindrome. Since every possible center is tested, the longest palindrome is among the expansions. Stopping at a mismatch cannot discard a longer palindrome with that same center.
longest-palindromic-substring.cost: There are roughly twice as many centers as characters. Each may expand across much of the string, giving quadratic work in the worst case. A few positions describe the expansion; the returned substring itself occupies output memory.
pitfalls: Try both odd and even centers.
Exclude the first mismatched outer pair.
Several equally long answers may be valid.

container-with-most-water.question: Which wall can we safely discard after measuring a container?
intuition: Every pair of walls gives a possible container, so checking all pairs takes quadratic work. The widest pair is a useful starting point, but width alone is not enough: the shorter wall sets the water level.

Imagine a horizontal waterline between two walls. Its height is limited by the shorter wall. Moving the taller wall inward would reduce width without raising that limit. Instead, discard the shorter wall and look for a taller replacement.
container-with-most-water.observation: Measure the area, then move a shorter wall inward. On equal heights, either wall can move.
approach: Begin at the two outermost walls.
Multiply their distance by the shorter height and remember the largest area.
Move the shorter side inward and repeat until the walls meet.
container-with-most-water.correctness: When a wall is shorter, every container using that wall and an interior opposite wall has less width and a water level no greater than its height. None can improve its measured area. Discarding that wall therefore loses no better answer. Repeating this safe elimination leaves the maximum among the measured pairs.
container-with-most-water.cost: Each move discards one wall, so there are fewer moves than walls. Only two positions and the largest area are remembered, giving linear work and constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Use the shorter height.
Width is the difference of wall positions.
Move a shorter wall only after recording its area.

3sum.question: How can sorted order turn a search for three numbers into a guided pair search?
intuition: Trying every triple repeats many combinations and can report the same values in different orders. Sorting gives us a direction: moving toward larger values increases a sum, while moving toward smaller values decreases it.

Hold one number fixed and balance the remaining pair from opposite ends of the sorted suffix. If the total is below zero, raise its smaller member. If it is above zero, lower its larger member. Equal choices at the same role can be skipped after a solution is recorded.
3sum.observation: Use three different positions, and skip equal values at the same choice level to avoid duplicate triplets.
approach: Sort the values and choose one fixed member.
Search the remaining suffix with a low and a high member, moving toward zero.
Record exact matches, skip repeated values, and repeat with the next distinct fixed member.
3sum.correctness: For a fixed first member, a sum below zero cannot be repaired by lowering the larger member, so the smaller member may safely advance. A sum above zero similarly requires lowering the larger member. These moves preserve every possible zero-sum pair. Trying each distinct first value covers all triplets; skipping equal role choices removes duplicates without removing distinct value combinations.
3sum.cost: For each fixed value, the pair search moves across the suffix once. With a linear number of fixed choices, total work is quadratic. A sorted copy uses linear extra memory, plus memory for the returned triplets.
pitfalls: Skip duplicate fixed values and duplicate pairs.
Use different positions even when values are equal.
Keep searching after the first match.

3sum-closest.question: How can we steer a triple toward a target even when no exact match exists?
intuition: Checking every triple gives a closest answer but performs many unguided comparisons. Once numbers are sorted, we can move a pair in a direction that predictably raises or lowers the triple total.

Fix one member and place the other two at opposite ends of the remaining sorted values. Measure the distance from the target before moving. A sum too small asks for a larger low member; a sum too large asks for a smaller high member. Keep the closest real total throughout.
3sum-closest.observation: Record each candidate distance before moving the pair; an exact match can finish immediately.
approach: Sort the values and initialize the closest total using a real triple.
For each fixed member, compare a low/high pair with the target.
Remember improvements and move the pair in the direction of the target.
3sum-closest.correctness: For a fixed member, when the sum is too small, keeping the smaller pair member and decreasing the larger one cannot bring it closer from below. The symmetric statement holds for a too-large sum. Measuring before each move preserves the best discarded candidate. Trying every fixed member therefore finds a globally closest triple.
3sum-closest.cost: Each fixed choice scans the suffix once, giving quadratic work. Sorting a copy uses linear memory. Only a few totals and positions are needed during each scan.
pitfalls: Initialize from a real triple, not an arbitrary zero.
Use three different positions.
Return the sum, not its distance from the target.

letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.question: What if each phone digit opens another set of letter doors?
intuition: The digits do not determine one word. Each offers several letters, and every choice at one position can combine with every choice at the next. Replacing digits independently without tracking their positions loses this product of choices.

Imagine a branching path: digit 2 offers a, b, or c; digit 3 then offers d, e, or f from each branch. A completed path spells one answer. Returning to an earlier fork lets us explore all remaining paths.
letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.observation: Choose exactly one permitted letter for each digit; save a word only after the last digit.
approach: Begin with an empty word.
For the next digit, explore each of its allowed letters as a continuation.
After all digits have contributed, save the completed word and return to explore other choices.
letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.correctness: A completed path chooses one allowed letter at each position, so every emitted word is valid. Any valid word specifies exactly one sequence of these position choices, and the branching search follows it. Thus all words are included without repeating a choice sequence.
letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.cost: Up to four choices at every digit produce exponentially many words. Writing each word also takes time proportional to its length. The reference holds copied prefixes during recursion, which can use quadratic auxiliary characters, in addition to the complete output.
pitfalls: Digits 7 and 9 have four letters.
Preserve the order of digit positions.
An empty input produces no words.

remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.question: Can two bookmarks locate a node counted from the far end?
intuition: A forward-only list gives no immediate position counted from its end. Counting the entire list first works, but a fixed gap between two bookmarks can reveal the desired predecessor in one coordinated walk.

Put a temporary starting node before the list. Move the front bookmark ahead by one more link than the requested end-distance. Then move both bookmarks together. When the front passes the end, the rear bookmark is just before the node to remove.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.observation: Keep a gap of one more link than the end-distance, measured from the temporary starting node.
approach: Place both bookmarks at a temporary node before the head.
Move the front bookmark ahead by the required gap, then move both together.
When the front passes the end, reconnect the rear node directly to the node after the one removed.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.correctness: The bookmarks start with a fixed separation and move the same distance, so that separation never changes. When the front has passed the end, the rear is exactly the needed distance before it: immediately before the target node. Bypassing that node preserves every other link and deletes exactly the requested node.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.cost: Each bookmark walks at most the list length. A temporary node and a few bookmarks use constant extra memory; the work is linear.
pitfalls: The gap must locate the predecessor.
Return the possibly changed first real node.
Count from the end, not from the beginning.

merge-two-sorted-lists.question: Why are just two exposed list heads enough to choose the next value?
intuition: Sorting every node again ignores the order already present in the two lists. The smallest remaining node of each list is always its head, so deeper nodes cannot be the next result while that head remains.

Imagine two ordered queues feeding one output chain. Compare their exposed front values and attach the smaller front node. Only that queue advances. When a queue empties, its counterpart’s remaining chain is already correctly ordered.
merge-two-sorted-lists.observation: Always attach a smallest exposed head, and advance only the list that supplied it.
approach: Compare the first remaining node of each list.
Attach the smaller node and expose its successor.
When one list ends, attach the rest of the other list.
merge-two-sorted-lists.correctness: Every time a node is attached, it is no larger than either list’s remaining head and hence no larger than any remaining node. The output therefore stays sorted. Advancing only its source uses every original node once. When one list empties, the other suffix is already ordered and belongs after the completed prefix.
merge-two-sorted-lists.cost: Each node is attached once, so work is proportional to the combined list lengths. Reusing the original nodes requires only a few bookmarks and one temporary starting node.
pitfalls: Advance the chosen source and the output tail.
Return the first real output node.
Preserve all equal-valued nodes.

generate-parentheses.question: How can a bracket string stay valid while we are still building it?
intuition: Generating all strings of opening and closing brackets wastes time on prefixes that are already impossible. A closing bracket cannot be repaired later if it appears before any available opening bracket.

Think of openings as pairs waiting to be closed. We may start a new pair while openings remain in our budget. We may close a pair only when one is currently waiting. Building under these rules keeps every prefix valid.
generate-parentheses.observation: Never close more pairs than have been opened, and never open more than the requested number of pairs.
approach: Begin with no pairs started or closed.
Explore a legal opening and a legal closing whenever each is available.
Save the string after all requested pairs have been opened and closed.
generate-parentheses.correctness: The construction rules ensure no prefix has more closings than openings and no result uses more than the pair budget. At completion, the counts agree, so every saved string is valid. Any valid string obeys these same prefix conditions, which means the search can follow all of its choices and will include it.
generate-parentheses.cost: Work grows with the number of valid bracket strings, multiplied by the length needed to write each one. The current path and recursion depth are linear in the number of pairs; the output contains all valid strings.
pitfalls: A completed string has twice as many characters as pairs.
A closing cannot appear without a waiting opening.
Undo a choice before exploring another branch.

merge-k-sorted-lists.question: Why does the next smallest node hide among just the exposed list heads?
intuition: Sorting all nodes again wastes the sorted order of each source. Comparing every source head after every output node also repeats work when many lists are present.

Each list exposes its smallest remaining node. Keep these exposed candidates in a small priority tournament, called a heap. Its winner is the next output node. Replace that winner with its successor from the same source.
merge-k-sorted-lists.observation: Only the next unused node of each nonempty list belongs in the tournament.
approach: Expose one head per nonempty list.
Take the smallest head, attach it, and expose its successor.
Repeat until every source is exhausted.
merge-k-sorted-lists.correctness: A tournament winner is no larger than any exposed head, and hence no larger than any hidden node. Attaching it preserves sorted order. Replacing it only with its own successor keeps one candidate per source. Repeating these two facts uses every node exactly once and yields the complete sorted chain.
merge-k-sorted-lists.cost: Scan the source heads once. Each output node then needs a logarithmic-size tournament update based on the number of lists. The candidate tournament stores at most one node per list.
pitfalls: Keep equal-valued nodes from different sources.
Expose the successor before changing output links.
Do not store every hidden node in the tournament.

swap-nodes-in-pairs.question: How can we exchange neighbors while keeping the rest of the chain attached?
intuition: Exchanging the printed values would not swap the original nodes. A node swap changes three connections, and changing them without preserving the continuation can detach the rest of the chain.

Treat the next two nodes as one small module. Remember the chain after it, reverse the pair’s internal order, and reconnect the incoming and outgoing links. The former first node becomes the predecessor for the next pair.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.observation: Swap only when two nodes remain; preserve the node after the pair before reconnecting.
approach: Locate the next pair and its following chain.
Reconnect the pair in opposite order between the same neighbors.
Advance beyond the swapped pair; leave a lone final node unchanged.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.correctness: Before each swap, the completed prefix already has the required pair ordering. The next two original nodes are reconnected in reverse order while their incoming link and continuation are preserved. This extends the correct prefix by two nodes without disturbing the suffix. A final lone node is not part of a pair and remains in place.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.cost: Each pair is reconnected once, giving linear work. A few node bookmarks and a temporary starting node use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Preserve the continuation before reconnecting.
The first real node may change.
Do not swap node values instead of nodes.

reverse-nodes-in-k-group.question: Why must we count a whole group before reversing its links?
intuition: Reversing nodes immediately upon arrival could also reverse a final group that is too short. The requirement treats that incomplete tail differently, so we need to know whether the group is complete first.

View the list as consecutive modules of the requested size. First check that an entire module exists. Reverse its internal links, reconnect it between its predecessor and continuation, then repeat. An incomplete module stays untouched.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.observation: Reverse only a complete group; inspect its size before changing any links.
approach: Check that the next group has the requested number of nodes.
Reverse that group’s links and reconnect its two boundaries.
Continue after the completed group; stop when fewer nodes remain.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.correctness: The completed prefix consists of exactly the full groups already reversed. Reversing the next complete module and restoring its two boundary links preserves every node and extends that prefix correctly. If the remaining suffix is too short, leaving it unchanged satisfies the special tail rule. These parts together cover the entire list.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.cost: Each node is inspected and relinked only a constant number of times. The total work is linear, with only a few bookmarks beyond the existing nodes.
pitfalls: Check group completeness before mutation.
Reconnect both incoming and outgoing group boundaries.
Leave the final short group in its original order.

substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.question: Can equal word lengths turn a letter scan into a moving bag of words?
intuition: Trying every start and recounting all its words repeats work. Equal word lengths give fixed-size chunks, but a valid start might be aligned at any letter position within one chunk width.

For each possible alignment, move a frame in whole-word chunks. Maintain how many copies of each required word it contains. Unknown chunks empty the frame; too many copies of a known word move the start forward until its count is allowed.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.observation: The frame must contain exactly the required number of copies of every word, not merely the right distinct words.
approach: Try each alignment within one word width.
Extend by a whole chunk, resetting on unknown words and shrinking excessive counts.
Record a start when the frame contains the full required word collection.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.correctness: Within one alignment, the frame contains only allowed chunks with counts no greater than required. Once its chunk count equals the required total, these bounded counts must all match exactly. Excess-count shrinking preserves all later valid starts, and reset discards only frames containing an impossible chunk. The alignment passes together examine all starts.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.cost: Each alignment advances forward in chunks. Including chunk slicing and counting, work is proportional to the text length times the word width. Remember counts for distinct words and the current framed collection.
pitfalls: Check every alignment within a word width.
Respect duplicate required words.
Shrink when a word is overrepresented, rather than discarding all potentially useful chunks.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array.question: How does a broken sorted row still let us discard half the search?
intuition: A rotation breaks the global sorted order, so ordinary midpoint comparisons alone are insufficient. Scanning works, but wastes a useful fact: around a midpoint, at least one side is still sorted.

Find the side that is sorted. Its two endpoint values tell whether the target could lie inside. Keep that side only if its range contains the target; otherwise keep the other side. Distinct values make the sorted-side decision unambiguous.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.observation: Use the sorted side’s value range to decide which half can contain the target.
approach: Inspect the middle value and return its position if it matches.
Identify a sorted half using the endpoint values.
Keep the half whose range can contain the target, and repeat.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.correctness: Rotation divides a distinct sorted row into at most two ordered runs. At each midpoint, one side lies within a single run. If its ordered endpoint range excludes the target, the entire side is impossible; if it includes the target, distinct sorted order excludes the opposite side. Each safe half-discard preserves the target when present.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.cost: Every decision removes roughly half the remaining candidates. Work grows logarithmically with row length, and only a few positions and boundary values are remembered.
pitfalls: Use inclusive and exclusive range boundaries consistently.
Return an original position, not the target value.
This method assumes distinct values.

sudoku-solver.question: Can choosing the most constrained empty square make Sudoku search smaller?
intuition: Filling empty squares in arbitrary order may branch into many guesses before noticing a conflict. A square with fewer legal digits supplies stronger information about what can work.

For each empty square, consider digits absent from its row, column, and three-by-three box. Choose the square with the fewest choices. Try a legal digit, continue, and erase it if no full board can follow. Fixed clues never change.
sudoku-solver.observation: A placed digit must be absent from all three containing groups; undo unsuccessful placements completely.
approach: Record digits already used in each row, column, and box.
Select an empty square with the fewest legal options and try each option.
Continue until the board is complete, undoing a trial when completion fails.
sudoku-solver.correctness: Every trial preserves the row, column, and box rules. Any full valid completion must choose one of the current square’s legal options, so trying all of them cannot miss that completion. Undoing a failed choice restores the earlier board before the next trial. A finished board is therefore valid and retains the fixed clues.
sudoku-solver.cost: Search can branch exponentially in the number of empty cells. Choosing the most constrained square reduces practical branching without changing that worst case. The fixed board, used-digit groups, and recursion bookmarks hold the current search state.
pitfalls: Never change an original clue.
Undo the board placement and all three used-digit records.
Choose only digits valid in the row, column, and box.

combination-sum.question: How do we count a combination once when its numbers can be reused?
intuition: Trying choices in every order would repeat the same collection: 2,2,3 and 3,2,2 are the same combination. The search needs an ordering rule as well as a target budget.

Sort the candidates and build a nondecreasing path. A chosen number may be used again, but later choices never return to a smaller value. Subtract each choice from the remaining budget; zero completes a combination.
combination-sum.observation: Allow reuse of the current value, but never return to a smaller choice along the same path.
approach: Sort the candidate values.
Choose a value that fits the remaining budget and continue with that value or a later one.
Save a combination when the budget becomes zero, then undo choices to explore alternatives.
combination-sum.correctness: Every path uses permitted candidates and reaches a zero remainder only when its sum equals the target. Every valid combination can be placed in nondecreasing order, and the search allows that ordered path, including repeated values. Restricting future choices to the same or larger values removes alternative orderings of the same collection.
combination-sum.cost: The search may explore exponentially many combinations, with depth bounded by the target divided by the smallest candidate. Current-path memory follows that depth; output memory depends on all saved combinations.
pitfalls: Permit reuse of a chosen value.
Do not emit different orders of the same collection.
Undo a choice before trying a sibling branch.

combination-sum-ii.question: How can equal candidates be used without producing duplicate combinations?
intuition: Equal-valued input positions can produce the same combination along different branches. Removing duplicate values entirely would also be wrong, because separate occurrences may both be needed.

Sort the occurrences. After choosing one, continue only beyond its position so that occurrence cannot be reused. At the same choice level, skip repeated values; deeper in the path, a later equal occurrence remains available.
combination-sum-ii.observation: Use each occurrence at most once; skip equal sibling choices, not equal values deeper in a combination.
approach: Sort occurrences and begin with the target budget.
Choose an occurrence and continue at later positions only.
Skip equal alternative choices at one level and save each zero-budget collection.
combination-sum-ii.correctness: Advancing past a chosen position enforces one use per occurrence. Sorting lets equal choices at the same level be recognized as interchangeable routes to the same value combination. Retaining the first such route covers every possible continuation, while equal values remain legal at deeper levels. Every saved path exactly spends the budget.
combination-sum-ii.cost: There can be exponentially many subsets to consider. Sorting costs extra preliminary work; the path and search depth are linear in input size, plus memory for all returned combinations.
pitfalls: Continue after the chosen occurrence.
Skip equal values only at the same choice level.
Keep separate equal occurrences when a combination needs them.

first-missing-positive.question: Could each small positive number mark its own parking space?
intuition: Sorting or keeping a separate membership collection would solve the problem but uses additional work or memory. With four input positions, a missing positive must be among 1 through 5; huge and negative values cannot be the smallest missing one.

Give each relevant value a home: 1 belongs in the first position, 2 in the second, and so on. Move a value into its home by exchanging it with what is there. Then the first home lacking its proper resident reveals the missing positive.
first-missing-positive.observation: Move only values within the available home range, and stop if their home already contains the same value.
approach: Place each value from one through the input length in its matching position.
Ignore negatives, zero, oversized values, and already placed duplicates.
Scan for the first missing resident; if every home is full, return one beyond the last home.
first-missing-positive.correctness: The answer is at most one more than the number of input positions: if all smaller positives are present, that next number is missing. Each successful exchange fills a value’s designated home and never needs to dislodge a correctly placed different value. After placement, a positive is present exactly when its home contains it, so the first failed home test gives the smallest missing positive.
first-missing-positive.cost: Although one position may trigger several exchanges, every successful exchange places another relevant value. There are only linearly many placements and one final scan. The original row supplies the memory, so auxiliary memory is constant.
pitfalls: Ignore zero and out-of-range values.
Stop on a duplicate already in its home.
Return one beyond the length if all homes are filled.

trapping-rain-water.question: Why does the lower known boundary settle water on its side?
intuition: A column can hold water only when higher boundaries exist on both sides. Checking both boundaries from scratch for every column repeats scans of the same skyline.

Walk inward from both ends while remembering the tallest boundary seen on each side. Resolve the side with the lower remembered boundary: the other side already supplies a wall at least that high. The difference between that boundary and the current column is its settled water depth.
trapping-rain-water.observation: Resolve the side with the lower known boundary; both boundaries are necessary to contain water.
approach: Track the tallest boundary encountered from each end.
On the side with the lower known boundary, add the depth above its current column.
Move inward and continue until every column’s contribution is settled.
trapping-rain-water.correctness: When one remembered boundary is lower, the opposite remembered boundary is already high enough to contain water at that level. The current column on the lower side can therefore be settled without knowing deeper interior walls. Moving inward accounts for that column exactly once. Repeated safe settlement sums precisely the contained water above every column.
trapping-rain-water.cost: Each move settles one column, so work is linear in the skyline length. Two positions, two remembered boundaries, and the running water total use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Use the lower of the two containing boundaries.
Count only water depth above a column.
Do not confuse trapped water with the largest single container.

permutations.question: What if every unused number could fill the next empty seat?
intuition: A complete ordering cannot reuse a number or leave one out. Generating arbitrary sequences and rejecting duplicates at the end wastes routes that were impossible as soon as a repeated choice appeared.

Build an ordering one seat at a time. At each seat, any unused number can be chosen. After exploring its continuations, release that choice so another branch can occupy the same seat. A full seating arrangement is one permutation.
permutations.observation: Each number occupies exactly one seat in a completed ordering.
approach: Choose any unused number for the next position.
Explore its continuations, then release it before the next alternative.
Save an independent copy when all positions are filled.
permutations.correctness: The unused-number rule ensures every completed route contains each input number exactly once. Every possible ordering gives a legal next choice at every seat, so its route is explored. Different routes first differ at some seat and therefore produce different permutations. Saving an independent result preserves it when later choices are undone.
permutations.cost: There are factorially many orderings, and writing each takes linear time in its length. Search bookmarks and the current path use linear auxiliary memory; storing the output dominates for large inputs.
pitfalls: Never reuse a number within one ordering.
Undo a branch before trying another.
Save copies rather than references to the changing path.

permutations-ii.question: How can equal numbers share a canonical order of choice?
intuition: Two equal values have different input positions but can produce the same final value ordering. A normal unused-position search would therefore repeat some permutations.

Sort the occurrences and require equal values to be chosen in their original sorted order within a path. A later copy may be used after an earlier copy is used. If the earlier copy is still free, choosing the later copy first would only duplicate that branch.
permutations-ii.observation: Among equal unused occurrences, choose the earliest one first.
approach: Sort occurrences and track which positions are used.
At each seat, choose an unused occurrence whose equal predecessor is already used.
Save each full ordering and undo choices to continue searching.
permutations-ii.correctness: Every distinct value ordering can assign its equal occurrences in their sorted occurrence order. That assignment is permitted by the rule, so no value ordering is missed. Any alternative assignment that picks a later free equal copy first is interchangeable with the canonical one and is rejected. Thus each distinct ordering is emitted once.

rotate-image.question: Can a quarter-turn be built from two reflections?
intuition: Copying every cell to a new matrix would make rotation easy but violates the in-place requirement. A rotation has a useful geometric decomposition that only exchanges existing cells.

First reflect the matrix across its main diagonal, exchanging row and column roles. Then reverse each row. Together, these reflections move every original cell to exactly its clockwise quarter-turn destination.
rotate-image.observation: Exchange each off-diagonal pair once, then reverse each row.
approach: Reflect across the top-left to bottom-right diagonal.
Reverse the order of cells within every row.
Keep the same matrix while its values move to their rotated positions.
rotate-image.correctness: Diagonal reflection moves a cell’s row coordinate to its column coordinate and vice versa. Reversing a reflected row then mirrors the new column coordinate across the row width. This is exactly the clockwise rotation rule for every cell. Both operations exchange values inside the original square matrix, preserving all cells and the matrix identity.
rotate-image.cost: Visit a constant number of times for each cell, giving work proportional to the square’s cell count. Only temporary exchange values are needed, so auxiliary memory is constant.
pitfalls: Reflect each off-diagonal pair only once.
Reverse rows after reflecting, to rotate clockwise.
Modify the original matrix rather than returning a separate copy.

n-queens.question: How can a queen placement prune every board that already contains an attack?
intuition: Trying every arrangement before checking attacks explores many doomed boards. Once two queens share a column or diagonal, later placements cannot repair their conflict.

Place one queen in each row. Remember occupied columns and the two kinds of diagonal. Explore only squares that avoid all three. When later rows have no safe square, remove the last queen and try another route.

Record its column and diagonals, then continue to the following row.
Save a full board, or undo a placement when exploring another branch.
n-queens.correctness: At each depth, all placed queens are mutually nonattacking. Adding a square outside occupied columns and diagonals preserves that fact. Every valid complete board supplies a legal next square in every row, so its route is explored. Undoing placements restores earlier availability. Complete routes are exactly valid boards.

pitfalls: Check both diagonal directions.
Remove all occupancy records when undoing.
Return complete boards, not merely queen coordinates.

maximum-subarray.question: When is it better to drop the past and start a new continuous section?
intuition: Checking every continuous section recomputes many overlapping sums. A negative accumulated prefix has a simple effect: it makes any section extended from it worse.

At each number, compare extending the previous section with starting fresh at this number. Keep the better total ending here, and separately remember the best total anywhere. This separates the local continuation from the historical answer.
maximum-subarray.observation: A negative preceding total cannot improve a section beginning at the current number.
approach: Start from the first value so negative-only inputs remain valid.
At each next value, choose between extending the current section and starting a new one.
Remember the greatest total reached at any ending position.
maximum-subarray.correctness: Any best section ending at a new number either contains only that number or extends a section ending immediately before it. Extending the best previous ending section is at least as good as extending any weaker one. Comparing these two possibilities therefore gives the exact best ending total. The maximum over all endings is the answer.
maximum-subarray.cost: Read each value once while remembering only the current ending total and the historical largest total. Work is linear, and extra memory is constant.
pitfalls: A section must be nonempty.
Return the historical best, not the final ending total.
Do not skip interior values; the section must be continuous.

spiral-matrix.question: Can peeling one rectangular border reveal the next spiral layer?
intuition: Moving in a spiral without remembering what remains risks revisiting corners or walking outside the grid. The unvisited cells always form a smaller rectangle after one complete outer layer.

Read the remaining rectangle’s top edge, right edge, bottom edge, and left edge in order. After each edge, move that boundary inward. Before reading an opposite edge, check that a row or column still remains.
spiral-matrix.observation: Read each boundary once and check that the remaining rectangle is not empty before its opposite edge.
approach: Read the top edge left to right, then the right edge downward.
If cells remain, read the bottom edge backward and the left edge upward.
Repeat with the shrunken rectangle until all boundaries cross.
spiral-matrix.correctness: At the beginning of each layer, the unvisited cells form the bounded rectangle. Reading an edge visits all of its cells exactly once, and moving that edge inward leaves precisely the remaining rectangle. Opposite-edge checks avoid revisiting cells when only one row or column remains. Repeating this invariant visits all cells in spiral order.
spiral-matrix.cost: Every cell is visited once. Four boundaries use constant auxiliary memory, while the returned traversal contains one entry per cell.
pitfalls: Do not visit a corner twice.
Check for a remaining row before the bottom edge.
Check for a remaining column before the left edge.

jump-game.question: Do we need a route, or only the farthest place any route can reach?
intuition: Trying every sequence of jumps revisits the same reachable positions. The question only asks whether the final position is reachable, so a full route history is unnecessary.

All positions up to the farthest reachable boundary form a reachable prefix. A jump from any position inside that prefix may extend its boundary. If the next position lies beyond it, no earlier jump can bridge the gap.
jump-game.observation: Only jumps from already reachable positions may extend the reachable boundary.
approach: Start with only the first position reachable.
For each position inside the reachable prefix, extend the boundary using its jump allowance.
Succeed when the boundary reaches the final position; fail at an unbridgeable gap.
jump-game.correctness: Initially only the start is reachable. A position inside the known prefix can be reached, and its allowed shorter jumps make every new position up to its farthest landing reachable too. Thus updating the boundary preserves an exactly reachable prefix. If a position lies beyond that prefix, every earlier jump ends before it, so no route can cross the gap.
jump-game.cost: Scan each position at most once. The farthest boundary and current position require constant extra memory; work is linear.
pitfalls: Ignore jump allowances at unreachable positions.
A zero is harmless if an earlier jump can pass it.
A one-position row is already at the goal.

merge-intervals.question: Why does sorting let the next range compare with just the latest merged range?
intuition: Comparing every interval with every other repeats overlap checks. Sorting by starting position orders the overlap groups so we can finish them one at a time.

Imagine painting coverage on a shared number line. Extend the current painted range whenever the next interval begins before that range ends. If the next start lies beyond the end, a real gap begins a new independent range.
merge-intervals.observation: An interval overlaps the latest range when its start is no greater than that range’s end.
approach: Sort intervals by their starting points.
Extend the current range through every overlap.
Start a separate range after a gap.
merge-intervals.correctness: Sorted starts mean all future intervals begin no earlier than the current one. When a gap appears after the current merged end, no later interval can reconnect to that finished component. Within a component, taking the larger end preserves exactly the union of overlapping ranges. The finished components therefore cover precisely the original intervals without gaps being added.
merge-intervals.cost: Sorting dominates with work proportional to the interval count times its logarithm. The later scan is linear. Sorting and the returned merged ranges require linear storage.
pitfalls: Sort before scanning.
Extend to the larger end, not simply the next end.
Use the problem’s closed-endpoint overlap rule.

rotate-list.question: Why does making a temporary circle simplify a list rotation?
intuition: Moving the last node to the front repeatedly would scan the chain many times. A rotation only changes where we begin reading the same cyclic node order.

Count the nodes and reduce the rotation by that length. Connect the tail back to the front to make a temporary circle. Find the node just before the desired new front, then break its outgoing link to restore a chain.
rotate-list.observation: A full-length rotation changes nothing; after choosing the new front, break the circle at its predecessor.
approach: Count the chain and reduce the shift by its length.
Connect the old tail to the old front.
Choose the new front and cut just before it.
rotate-list.correctness: Closing the tail-to-front link creates a circle containing every original node exactly once. Selecting the new front preserves this cyclic order while changing the linear reading start. Cutting its predecessor’s link yields exactly the desired suffix followed by the original prefix, with every node present and no cycle left.
rotate-list.cost: Counting and finding the cut each walk across at most the list length. A few bookmarks use constant extra memory, so total work is linear.
pitfalls: Break the temporary circle before returning.
Reduce large shifts by the list length.
Handle empty and single-node chains before making a circle.

unique-paths.question: How can route counts flow through a grid without listing the routes?
intuition: Listing all right-and-down routes repeats the same smaller path problem at many shared cells. We need only the number of routes reaching each cell.

Each arrival comes either from above or from the left. These two groups have different last moves, so their counts add without duplication. Process cells after their predecessor counts are known. A single remembered row is enough.
unique-paths.observation: Add the above and left counts; neither group overlaps the other because their last moves differ.
approach: Give each top-row and left-column cell its one boundary route.
Add the two predecessor counts at each interior cell.
Read the count at the destination.
unique-paths.correctness: A route to an interior cell has a unique final move, either right from the left cell or down from the above cell. Removing that move gives a route counted at its predecessor, and adding it reconstructs exactly one arrival route. The two groups are disjoint and complete, so adding their correct smaller counts gives the exact cell count.
unique-paths.cost: Compute one count per cell, giving work proportional to the grid area. The reference remembers a row along the shorter dimension, so auxiliary memory grows only with that dimension.
pitfalls: Count routes, not just reachable cells.
Above and left counts must already be known.
A single-row grid still has one route.

climbing-stairs.question: Why do the last one-step and two-step moves partition every route?
intuition: Listing every sequence of one-step and two-step moves grows quickly and repeats the route-count question for the same stair. The final move gives a simpler decomposition.

Every route to a stair arrives from one stair below with a one-step move, or from two stairs below with a two-step move. These groups cannot overlap because their last moves differ. Add their already known counts.
climbing-stairs.observation: The count for a stair is the sum of the counts for its two possible predecessor stairs.
approach: Begin with one route to stay at the ground and one route to reach the first stair.

Return the count for the requested stair.

Starting from correct base counts, repeated addition gives the exact answer.

set-matrix-zeroes.question: Why must we remember original zeros before making new ones?
intuition: Clearing a row immediately after finding a zero creates more zeros. Treating those new zeros as original evidence could clear unrelated rows and columns.

Separate discovery from clearing. Use the first row and first column as marker strips for interior zeros, and separately remember whether those marker strips originally contained zeros. Once all evidence is recorded, apply it in a second pass.

Mark affected rows and columns using their boundary cells.
Clear interior cells from the markers, then apply the remembered boundary obligations.
set-matrix-zeroes.correctness: During discovery, each interior original zero marks exactly its row and column. Separate flags preserve the original status of the marker strips. Applying these records clears a cell exactly when its row or column originally contained a zero. New zeros never add obligations, so unrelated cells remain unchanged.
set-matrix-zeroes.cost: Two passes visit the matrix cells a constant number of times, giving work proportional to its area. The existing boundary cells and two flags provide constant auxiliary memory.
pitfalls: Record original first-row and first-column status.
Do not let newly created zeros trigger more clearing.
Keep discovery and application separate.

intuition: A cell-by-cell scan ignores the order across row boundaries. Each row starts after the previous row ends, so the entire row-major sequence is sorted.
Imagine numbering all cells along a ribbon, continuing from one row to the next. Search the middle numbered position and translate it back into a row and column only when reading a value.

approach: Treat row-major cell positions as a single ordered search range.

Return whether a matching value is found.
search-a-2d-matrix.correctness: The row-order contract makes the imagined ribbon globally sorted. A midpoint comparison therefore removes only values that cannot equal the target. Translating a numbered position into row and column identifies the same original cell, so the surviving match or exhausted range gives the correct membership answer.
search-a-2d-matrix.cost: Each comparison halves the remaining cell positions, giving logarithmic work in the cell count. Only a few numbered positions are stored.
pitfalls: The row boundary ordering makes every earlier ribbon value smaller than a later one.

minimum-window-substring.question: How can a covering frame become as narrow as possible?
intuition: Recounting every substring repeats character work. A valid covering section may also contain unnecessary letters or extra copies that can be removed from its beginning.

Grow a frame until it includes every required character copy. Then shrink its beginning while the coverage remains complete. Record the narrowest complete frame before releasing a required copy forces growth again.

approach: Grow until all required copies are covered.
Shrink while coverage stays valid, recording shorter answers.
Grow again after a required copy is released.
minimum-window-substring.correctness: For each ending position, shrinking while coverage holds finds its shortest valid starting position. Any further shrink loses a required copy. Growth preserves all later possibilities, and every valid ending is considered. Remembering the smallest length among these locally shortest frames yields the global minimum.
minimum-window-substring.cost: The frame edges move forward only. Each character enters and leaves at most once, giving linear work in both strings’ lengths and memory for character counts.
pitfalls: Coverage counts every required copy; shrink only while none is missing.
Use occurrence counts rather than a membership set.

combinations.correctness: Every selection of distinct values has exactly one increasing order. The search follows that order and no reordered alternative. combinations.cost: Writing each result takes time proportional to the requested selection size. Search-path memory is linear in that size; output contains all binomially many selections.
pitfalls: Choose later numbers only, and prune when too few remain.

word-search.question: Can a word be spelled along one path without revisiting a square?
intuition: Letter counts alone cannot establish a word: its letters must be adjacent in order. A promising partial route may also become impossible, so cells must be released when exploring another route.

Start from a matching first letter. Walk through side-adjacent matching letters, temporarily reserving each visited square. If a continuation fails, release its squares and try another neighbor. A reservation belongs only to its current path.
word-search.observation: A cell can be used once within a path; moves must share a side and match the next letter.
approach: Try matching first-letter cells.
Reserve a matching square and explore side neighbors for the next letter.
Restore on return; succeed after all letters are matched.
word-search.correctness: Each explored path matches a prefix of the requested word and uses distinct adjacent cells. Trying every legal matching neighbor includes the next move of any valid full path. Releasing cells after a branch restores the board for other starts and routes. Completing every letter therefore proves existence; exhausting the starts proves absence.
word-search.cost: Try each starting cell, then potentially several neighbors for each next letter. Worst-case work is exponential in word length times board area. The current reserved path needs memory proportional to its length.
pitfalls: A cell can be used once within a path; moves must share a side and match the next letter.
Matching counts cannot override the one-use rule.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.question: What if duplicates hide which half of a rotated row is sorted?
intuition: The distinct-value search relies on recognizing a sorted side. Equal endpoints and midpoint can hide the rotation break, so confidently discarding half may lose the target.

First test the middle for equality with the target. If both endpoints equal that nonmatching middle, remove those endpoints: they are known not to be the target. Once the ambiguity clears, use the ordered half’s endpoint range.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.observation: Trim ambiguous equal endpoints only after confirming they are not the target.
approach: Test the midpoint.
Trim equal nonmatching endpoints when the sorted side is hidden.
Otherwise keep the half whose ordered range can contain the target.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.correctness: Endpoint trimming removes only values already known unequal to the target. A visible sorted side can be safely included or excluded by its value range. Both operations preserve the target if it exists. The range eventually finds the target or becomes empty.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.cost: Clear sorted halves permit logarithmic searching, but repeated equal endpoints can require linear work in the worst case. A few boundary positions use constant memory.
pitfalls: Trim ambiguous equal endpoints only after confirming they are not the target.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.question: Why can each equal-value run keep just its first node?
intuition: A general duplicate search would need to remember all values. Sorted order makes equal values neighboring nodes, so the next node is the only duplicate candidate that matters.

Keep the current node as the representative of its equal run. If the next value matches, bypass that next node and inspect the new successor. Advance the representative only after its successor has a different value.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.observation: After bypassing a duplicate, stay at the representative to check for further duplicates.
approach: Compare the representative with its successor.
Bypass equal successors without advancing.
Advance only to a different value.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.correctness: Each representative is the first surviving node of one sorted equal run. Repeated bypasses remove precisely its equal successors. Advancing at a different value starts the next run. Thus every original value retains exactly one node and the surviving chain stays sorted.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.cost: Each node is inspected or bypassed once. A single current-node bookmark uses constant memory, and total work is linear.
pitfalls: After bypassing a duplicate, stay at the representative to check for further duplicates.
Advancing after the first removal would leave a duplicate.

subsets-ii.question: How can later equal copies remain useful while equal sibling choices disappear?
intuition: Equal occurrences can start identical families of subsets. Removing them entirely would lose subsets that need two copies, while exploring every equal sibling would duplicate results.

Sort the values. At any one selection step, try only the first of equal alternatives. Once a value is chosen, its later equal copy may still be chosen deeper in that path. Save each path, including empty.
subsets-ii.observation: Skip equal choices at the same depth, while permitting equal copies at deeper depths.
approach: Sort equal values together.
Save the path and extend through later positions.
Skip equal sibling choices, then undo each extension.
subsets-ii.correctness: Every multiset subset can be built by taking its equal occurrences in sorted order. The earliest sibling choice permits all later copies as descendants, so it covers every needed multiplicity. Repeating a later equal sibling would cover the same family and is skipped. Every saved path therefore represents one distinct subset.
subsets-ii.cost: Worst-case output remains exponential when values are distinct. Sorting and the current path add linear-size working storage; copied subsets account for the output size.
pitfalls: Skip equal choices at the same depth, while permitting equal copies at deeper depths.
Keeping multiple copies differs from repeating the same subset.

decode-ways.question: Can the last one-digit or two-digit letter explain every decoding?
intuition: A greedy first split can miss other valid interpretations, and zeros make some pieces invalid. Repeatedly trying all full splits also revisits the same prefixes.

At each prefix ending, consider a final one-digit code from 1 through 9 and a final two-digit code from 10 through 26. Each legal ending adds the count of ways to decode the earlier prefix. Keep these prefix counts for reuse.
decode-ways.observation: Zero is never a one-digit letter; a two-digit ending must be between 10 and 26.
approach: Start with one empty-prefix decoding.
Add the counts for legal one-digit and two-digit endings.
Read the full-prefix count.
decode-ways.correctness: Every decoding ends with exactly one legal one-digit or two-digit code. Removing it gives a decoding of the corresponding earlier prefix. These two groups are disjoint, and adding the final code reconstructs each full decoding uniquely. Correct base counts and repeated addition therefore count every decoding exactly once.
decode-ways.cost: Each prefix makes at most two ending checks, giving linear work. This reference retains the prefix-count table, so memory is linear as well.
pitfalls: Zero is never a one-digit letter; a two-digit ending must be between 10 and 26.
Leading zero pieces are invalid.

reverse-linked-list-ii.question: Can we reverse one chain section by repeatedly moving its next node to the front?
intuition: Reversing the whole list would disturb nodes outside the requested section. A local reversal must preserve the connections both before and after that section.

Keep the node before the section fixed. The original first section node becomes its eventual tail. Repeatedly remove the node just after that tail and insert it at the section front. Each move extends the reversed section by one.
reverse-linked-list-ii.observation: Only section nodes move; keep its predecessor fixed and preserve the continuing suffix.
approach: Find the node before the section.
Move the next unprocessed section node to the section front.
Repeat until the specified section is reversed.
reverse-linked-list-ii.correctness: After each move, the nodes already transferred form the reversed beginning of the section, ending at its original first node. Removing its next node and placing that node at the front extends this reversed prefix while preserving the outside links. Exactly one fewer move than section length transfers all remaining section nodes into reverse order.
reverse-linked-list-ii.cost: Finding the section and transferring its nodes takes linear worst-case work in the list length. A few node bookmarks use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Only section nodes move; keep its predecessor fixed and preserve the continuing suffix.
A section of length one is already reversed.

validate-binary-search-tree.question: Why must a node obey all ancestor bounds, rather than just its parent?
intuition: A child may look correct beside its parent yet violate a more distant ancestor’s ordering rule. Checking only adjacent values misses that inherited restriction.
Carry an allowed open interval down the tree. A left child inherits a smaller upper limit, while a right child inherits a larger lower limit. A node must fall strictly between every inherited bound.
validate-binary-search-tree.observation: The allowed interval is strict and contains all ancestor restrictions.
approach: Visit a node with its inherited lower and upper bounds.
Reject a value outside those strict bounds.
Pass narrowed bounds to the children.
validate-binary-search-tree.correctness: The root has unrestricted bounds. Each child receives the intersection of inherited ancestor bounds with its parent’s new restriction. If every node passes, every left-subtree value is smaller and every right-subtree value is larger than each ancestor it depends on. Conversely, any violated search-tree rule produces a failed inherited bound.
validate-binary-search-tree.cost: Visit each node once. The iterative depth-first frontier uses memory proportional to tree height in the worst case.
pitfalls: The allowed interval is strict and contains all ancestor restrictions.
The value 4 also has to exceed ancestor 5.

same-tree.question: What must match besides the values when comparing two trees?
intuition: Two trees may contain the same values but connect them differently. Comparing traversed values without missing-child positions loses their shape.

Compare paired positions from the two roots. Two missing positions match; one missing position and one real node do not. Real nodes must have equal values, then their corresponding left and right positions must also match.
same-tree.observation: Compare both shape and values at corresponding positions.
approach: Compare the two current positions.
Reject unequal values or one-sided absence.
Continue with both corresponding child pairs.
same-tree.correctness: The search compares the roots and then exactly corresponding descendant positions. Any unequal value or asymmetric absence rejects equality. If all paired positions agree, the trees have identical structure and values. Every tree position is eventually paired, so no structural difference can be overlooked.
same-tree.cost: Each paired node position is visited at most once. Work is linear in the trees’ combined size; the depth-first pending pairs use memory proportional to their height.
pitfalls: Compare both shape and values at corresponding positions.
Equal multisets of values do not establish equal shape.

binary-tree-level-order-traversal.question: How can a queue keep children out of their parents’ level?
intuition: A single traversal sequence does not group nodes by depth. Newly discovered children must wait while all nodes of the current level are processed.

At a level’s beginning, freeze the number of nodes already waiting. Process exactly that group, adding its children behind them for the next level. The queue naturally keeps shallower nodes before deeper nodes.
binary-tree-level-order-traversal.observation: Freeze the current level size before appending children.
approach: Freeze the queue size for this level.
Process that many nodes and enqueue children left to right.
Save the level and repeat.
binary-tree-level-order-traversal.correctness: Initially the queue contains exactly the root level. Processing its frozen size removes all and only that level’s nodes, while their children form the next queue group in left-to-right order. Repeating this fact yields precisely the tree’s levels without mixing depths.
binary-tree-level-order-traversal.cost: Visit each node once. The queue stores at most a tree-width-sized frontier; the returned level groups store all node values.
pitfalls: Freeze the current level size before appending children.
Do not create a level containing a missing root.
