binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.question: Can alternating output direction leave the traversal queue simple?
intuition: Alternating how children enter the queue makes parent and child order harder to reason about. Only the displayed direction needs to alternate.

Collect each level left to right using ordinary queue order. Reverse its collected values on every other level, while continuing to enqueue children left to right. Output direction and traversal direction are separate concerns.
binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.observation: Reverse alternating result groups; keep child queue order consistently left to right.
approach: Collect the current level left to right.
Reverse its values when this level’s direction is backward.
Toggle direction and continue with the next level.
binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.correctness: Ordinary breadth-first grouping gives each level’s true left-to-right values. Applying the required display direction to each group changes only that group’s ordering. Since queue traversal remains consistent, subsequent level groups are still correct, and alternating the display flag produces the zigzag result.
binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.cost: Every node is visited once and every level is reversed at most once. Queue memory follows tree width; all displayed values occupy output memory.
pitfalls: Reverse alternating result groups; keep child queue order consistently left to right.
Direction changes happen per level, not per node.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.question: How do arrival order and left-to-right order reveal the same tree?
intuition: Neither preorder nor inorder alone identifies all parent-child links. Together they tell us which node arrives next and when an ancestor’s left side has finished.

Read new nodes in preorder, which visits parents before descendants. Keep unfinished ancestors. Inorder visits left subtree, root, right subtree; when an ancestor matches the next inorder value, its left portion is complete and we can move toward its right portion.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.observation: Create nodes in preorder, and close completed ancestor positions in inorder.
approach: Create the first preorder value as the root.
Attach left descendants while inorder has not closed the ancestor.
Close matching ancestors and attach the next right subtree.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.correctness: Preorder supplies each subtree root before any of its descendants. Inorder tells when the left descendants and that root have been fully visited. The stack preserves the unfinished ancestor chain, so closing matching ancestors identifies exactly where the next right subtree belongs. With distinct values, these traversal positions uniquely determine the reconstructed tree.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.cost: Each value is created once and each unfinished ancestor is removed once, giving linear work. The ancestor stack follows tree height; new tree nodes are output memory.
pitfalls: Create nodes in preorder, and close completed ancestor positions in inorder.
The two traversal sequences describe the same distinct node values.

minimum-depth-of-binary-tree.question: Why is the first leaf in breadth-first order the shortest completed path?
intuition: A missing child is not a completed root-to-leaf path when its sibling exists. Computing a minimum through empty branches can therefore give an impossibly short depth.
Visit nodes in order of increasing depth using a queue. The first node with no children is a genuine leaf and completes the shortest root path. Return its depth immediately.
minimum-depth-of-binary-tree.observation: A leaf has neither child. One missing child does not make a node a leaf.
approach: Queue the root with depth one.
Visit nodes in increasing depth.
Return the first genuine leaf’s depth.
minimum-depth-of-binary-tree.correctness: Breadth-first order processes every node at a smaller depth before any node at a greater depth. Therefore the first genuine leaf has a depth no greater than any other leaf. Requiring both children absent ensures the chosen endpoint is a valid complete path rather than an empty branch.
minimum-depth-of-binary-tree.cost: In the worst case, visit every node. The queue uses memory proportional to the widest frontier; early return can avoid deeper work.
pitfalls: A leaf has neither child. One missing child does not make a node a leaf.
The missing sibling does not create a zero-length leaf path.

intuition: A partial path can reach the target before reaching a leaf, which does not satisfy this task. Recomputing each full path’s total also repeats shared ancestors.
Carry the running sum down each branch. Add a child’s value to the inherited sum. Check equality only when both children are absent. Different branches keep their own totals.

path-sum.cost: Visit each node once. Depth-first pending branch totals require memory proportional to tree height; no full paths need to be copied.
pitfalls: Check the target only at leaves.
Do not discard a branch solely because its partial total exceeds the target.
Keep branch totals independent.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.question: What is the only earlier buying price a selling day needs to remember?
intuition: Checking every earlier purchase for every selling day repeats comparisons. For a fixed sale, a higher earlier buying price can never beat a lower earlier one.

Treat each day as a possible sale. Remember the cheapest price seen before it and compare today’s sale with that price. Separately remember the best profit already seen; doing no trade keeps profit zero.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.observation: A purchase must precede its sale; the best earlier purchase is the cheapest earlier price.
approach: Remember the first price as the earliest buying opportunity.
For each later day, compare selling today against the earlier minimum.
Update the best profit and the cheapest price for future days.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.correctness: For any selling day, subtracting the lowest earlier price gives the greatest legal profit on that day. The scan maintains that exact earlier minimum, so it considers the best trade ending on each day. Taking the maximum across those daily candidates and zero yields the best single legal trade or no trade.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.cost: Read every price once. The cheapest earlier price and largest profit use constant extra memory, giving linear time.
pitfalls: Do not buy after selling.
Use one transaction only.
Return zero when every legal trade loses money.

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.question: Why can a completed path use two branches, while an upward extension can use only one?
intuition: A best path need not pass through the root. Also, sending two child branches upward would create a fork, which is not a single path.

At each node, compare a completed path passing through it with both useful child branches. But offer its parent only the node plus one best child branch. A negative child contribution can be omitted; the completed answer must still contain a node.
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.observation: A path offered upward has one child branch at most; a completed path may join both branches through its center.
approach: Compute child contributions after their subtrees are processed.
Compare the node plus both positive child contributions with the best complete path.
Offer the parent the node plus at most one useful child contribution.
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.correctness: Every path has a highest node where its two downward sides, if any, meet. Considering the best useful contribution from each child at that node covers the best path with that center. Upward offers remain single paths by using at most one child. Comparing completed candidates at every node therefore finds the global maximum without creating forks.
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.cost: Process each node once after its children. This reference stores computed contributions and an explicit traversal state, so its auxiliary memory is linear in node count.
pitfalls: Do not send two child branches upward.
A best path need not contain the root.
Initialize the completed answer to handle all-negative trees.

longest-consecutive-sequence.question: Why should a consecutive run begin only where its predecessor is missing?
intuition: Starting a count at every present value repeatedly walks the same long run. Sorting would avoid that repetition but uses more time than membership checks need.

Put distinct values in a membership set. Begin walking upward only from a value whose predecessor is absent. Such a value is the unique beginning of its consecutive run; interior values can be skipped as starts.
longest-consecutive-sequence.observation: Start a run only when its immediately smaller value is absent.
approach: Build a membership set of the values.
From each value with no predecessor, count upward until the next value is absent.
Keep the longest counted run.
longest-consecutive-sequence.correctness: Each maximal consecutive run has exactly one value lacking a predecessor. The method starts there and walks every value in that run once. Skipping all other starts prevents repeated run walks but loses no run. Taking the greatest counted length therefore gives the correct result.
longest-consecutive-sequence.cost: Membership operations take constant expected time. Every distinct value is walked in one run and tested as a possible start, giving expected linear work and linear set memory.
pitfalls: Consecutive values need not be adjacent in the input.
Skip starts whose predecessor exists.
Duplicates do not add to run length.

intuition: A partition search may inspect the same substring’s mirrored characters repeatedly from different routes. Testing those pieces once separates the mirror question from the cut-placement question.

First record which continuous ranges read the same forward and backward. Then choose a palindromic first piece, continue after its end, and explore every legal next cut. A completed sequence of pieces covers the string exactly.

Save complete partitions and undo pieces to explore other cuts.

palindrome-partitioning.cost: Mirror-range preprocessing uses quadratic work and memory. The number of partitions can be exponential, and writing their pieces adds output-sized work. Search depth is bounded by string length.

gas-station.question: Why does a failed fuel stretch eliminate every start inside that stretch?
intuition: Trying a full lap from every station repeats the same deficits. A failure before finishing the lap gives stronger information than just one bad starting station.

Track fuel gained minus fuel spent. When a candidate stretch first runs negative, its current start fails. Every intermediate start also fails by that point: removing a nonnegative initial prefix cannot improve the remaining balance. Begin again after the failure.
gas-station.observation: A negative total net fuel makes every start impossible; a failed candidate stretch can restart only after its failure.
approach: Accumulate both full-circle net fuel and the current candidate tank.
When the candidate tank becomes negative, restart after that station.
Return the surviving start only if the full-circle total is nonnegative.
gas-station.correctness: Before a stretch’s first failure, its earlier partial balances are nonnegative. Starting later inside that stretch removes one such nonnegative prefix, so its balance at the failing end cannot improve enough to become nonnegative. All those starts may be discarded. If the total circle balance is nonnegative, the final surviving candidate also has enough surplus to cover the earlier discarded deficit portion after wrapping.
gas-station.cost: One scan updates the full-circle balance, candidate balance, and start position. Work is linear and extra memory is constant.
pitfalls: Check the full-circle total before returning.
Restart after the failed station.
Do not confuse station fuel with its net fuel gain.

single-number.question: How can equal pairs cancel without remembering where they appeared?
intuition: A frequency table would find the lone value but stores counts for many numbers. The exact promise that every other value appears twice allows a cancellation identity.

XOR compares bits, producing one where the input bits differ. Two identical bit patterns XOR to zero, and zero changes nothing when XORed with another pattern. Order does not matter, so all paired values cancel and leave the lone value.
single-number.observation: XOR all values; identical pairs cancel, while the unpaired value remains.
approach: Begin with the zero bit pattern.
XOR each input value into the running pattern.
Return the remaining pattern after all pairs cancel.
single-number.correctness: XOR is associative and commutative, so the combined pattern can be regrouped into identical pairs without changing its value. Each pair reduces to zero, and combining zeros leaves the lone input value unchanged. The result is therefore exactly the unique single occurrence under the problem’s frequency promise.
single-number.cost: One XOR per value gives linear work. The running bit pattern uses constant extra memory under the stated integer domain.
pitfalls: Use XOR, not addition or logical comparison.
The twice-except-once frequency promise is essential.
Input order does not affect cancellation.

word-break.question: Why must we remember several possible word boundaries instead of choosing one long word?
intuition: A greedy word choice can leave an impossible suffix even when another split succeeds. Retrying all prefix splits recursively also repeats the same boundary questions.

Imagine positions between characters as landing points. The start is reachable. A dictionary word can connect a reachable boundary to another boundary. Keep all reachable positions, so a later word can build on any valid earlier split.
word-break.observation: A boundary is reachable only through a whole dictionary word from an already reachable boundary.
approach: Mark the start boundary reachable.
At each later boundary, check dictionary pieces from earlier reachable boundaries.
Return whether the final boundary becomes reachable.
word-break.correctness: A marked boundary has a valid dictionary-word partition of its preceding text. Extending it with a dictionary word preserves that fact. Every valid full partition supplies a sequence of such boundary connections, so its final boundary will be marked. Thus final reachability is equivalent to the requested segmentation.
word-break.cost: The reference checks bounded-length candidate pieces at each end, including the cost of creating and hashing those pieces. Memory stores reachable boundaries and the dictionary rather than repeated full partition histories.
pitfalls: Do not commit greedily to the longest matching word.
Dictionary words may be reused.
Require reachability of the final boundary.

linked-list-cycle.question: Can a faster walker catch a slower walker only when the chain loops?
intuition: Remembering every visited node detects revisits but needs growing memory. Two walking speeds exploit the structure of a loop without storing the entire history.

Move one bookmark one link per round and another two links. If the faster one reaches an end, no loop exists. Inside a loop, their relative separation changes by one node per round, so they eventually coincide.
linked-list-cycle.observation: Compare the same node identity, not merely equal stored values.
approach: Move one bookmark by one link and the other by two.
Return no if the faster bookmark reaches an end.
Return yes when both bookmarks refer to the same node after moving.
linked-list-cycle.correctness: Without a cycle, advancing along next links eventually ends, so the fast walker cannot keep going or meet the slow walker after moving. In a cycle, both eventually enter it. The fast walker advances one extra link relative to the slow walker each round; modulo the cycle length, it visits every possible separation and reaches zero. Their meeting therefore detects exactly a cycle.
linked-list-cycle.cost: The walkers traverse a linear number of links before ending or meeting. Two bookmarks use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Compare node identities.
Check the fast walker can take both links.
Do not treat their shared initial position as a detected cycle.

linked-list-cycle-ii.question: Why is the first meeting inside a loop different from its entrance?
intuition: A slow-fast meeting proves a cycle but may happen anywhere inside it. Returning that meeting directly can identify the wrong node.
After detecting a meeting, place one bookmark back at the start. Move it and the meeting bookmark one link per round. The loop-distance relationship makes their next meeting occur at the entrance.
linked-list-cycle-ii.observation: The detection meeting is not the answer; equal-speed walkers locate the entrance afterward.
approach: Detect a meeting with one-link and two-link walkers.
Restart one bookmark at the original head.
Move both one link until their node identities match.
linked-list-cycle-ii.correctness: At detection, the fast walker has traveled twice the slow distance, so the extra traveled distance is a whole number of loop lengths. This makes the distance from the meeting to the entrance, modulo the loop length, equal to the head-to-entrance distance. Equal-speed walkers from those two starting points therefore first meet at the entrance.
linked-list-cycle-ii.cost: Detection and entrance location each require only linear link traversal. A few node bookmarks use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Do not return the initial detection meeting.
Keep node identity in both phases.
Acyclic lists have no entrance.

reorder-list.question: How do two forward-moving chains simulate alternating front and back choices?
intuition: A singly linked list cannot walk backward from its tail. Repeatedly finding the tail would require many rescans.

Split the list near the middle. Reverse the second half so its forward order now follows the original list backward. Then weave one node from the first half and one from the reversed half alternately.
reorder-list.observation: Detach the halves before reversal and preserve each next link while weaving.
approach: Find the middle and split into two chains.
Reverse the second chain.
Alternate nodes from the first and reversed second chains.
reorder-list.correctness: The first half lists the original front nodes in order, and the reversed second half lists the original back nodes in reverse order. Alternating these sequences therefore produces exactly the required first-last-second-next-last pattern. Detaching and preserving continuations ensures every original node is used once and the final chain terminates.
reorder-list.cost: Finding the middle, reversing, and weaving each take linear work. Only node bookmarks beyond the original chain are needed.
pitfalls: Detach the original halves before weaving, so old links cannot create a cycle.
Preserve both continuations before weaving links.
Change links rather than copying values.

sort-list.question: Can sorted one-node runs grow into a sorted whole chain?
intuition: Copying all values into an array and sorting would use linear extra memory. Recursive merging may also require call-stack memory. Bottom-up merging works directly with links.

One-node sections are already sorted. Merge neighboring sections of length one, then two, then four, doubling the known sorted run size after each full pass. Reconnect each merged run into the original chain.
sort-list.observation: At each pass, merge only neighboring sorted runs of the current size.
approach: Count nodes and begin with run size one.
Cut neighboring runs, merge their exposed minima, and reconnect them.
Double the run size until one sorted run spans the chain.
sort-list.correctness: Initially each size-one run is sorted. Merging two sorted neighboring runs by their exposed minima produces a sorted combined run containing exactly their nodes. A full pass therefore doubles the sorted run size. Once that size spans the node count, the entire chain is one sorted run, preserving every original node.
sort-list.cost: Every pass processes all nodes and the run size doubles, giving logarithmically many passes and overall linear-times-logarithmic work. Bottom-up link merging uses constant auxiliary memory.
pitfalls: Detach run boundaries before merging.
Reconnect the output tail after every pair.
Do not claim constant memory for a copied array.

maximum-product-subarray.question: Why might the worst negative product become tomorrow’s best positive product?
intuition: Remembering only the greatest product ending here loses useful negative history. Multiplying by another negative can reverse the order of best and worst candidates.

Keep both the greatest and least products ending at the current position. The next value may start fresh, extend the greatest, or extend the least. Compare all three and retain both new extremes, plus the historical greatest product.
maximum-product-subarray.observation: Use both previous extremes when multiplying by the next value.
approach: Initialize both ending extremes from the first value.
Compare starting fresh with extending each previous extreme.
Update both extremes and the historical maximum.
maximum-product-subarray.correctness: Every section ending at a new value either starts there or extends a previous ending section. A positive multiplier preserves product order and a negative reverses it, so the prior greatest and least products cover both possibilities. Comparing those extensions and a restart gives exact new extremes. The greatest historical ending product is the overall answer.
maximum-product-subarray.cost: Three candidate products per value give linear work. Two ending extremes and one historical answer use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Remember the least product as well as the greatest.
Compute new extremes from the previous extremes.
Handle zero and all-negative inputs without an empty section.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.question: What does the midpoint tell us when compared with the final candidate value?
intuition: The smallest value may lie at the rotation break, so the first element is not necessarily the answer. A linear scan ignores the two sorted runs.

Compare the midpoint with the range’s last value. A larger midpoint lies in the high run, so the minimum is strictly to its right. Otherwise, the midpoint lies in the low ordered side and may itself be the minimum.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.observation: Discard a high-run midpoint, but retain a low-run midpoint as a candidate.
approach: Compare the middle and last candidate values.
If the middle is larger, keep only values after it.
Otherwise keep the middle and the range before it; stop at one candidate.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.correctness: The distinct rotated row has a high run followed by a low run, or is already fully sorted. Comparing a midpoint to the current right endpoint identifies whether the minimum must occur beyond the midpoint or can occur at or before it. Each update preserves the minimum, and a single remaining candidate must be it.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.cost: Each comparison removes about half the candidates. Work is logarithmic and remembered boundaries use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Keep the midpoint in the low-side case.
This version assumes distinct values.
Return the value, not its position.

majority-element.question: Why can a strict majority survive cancellation of unlike pairs?
intuition: A frequency table remembers every distinct value. The stronger promise that one value appears more than half the time lets opposing votes cancel without retaining all counts.

Maintain one candidate and a balance of unmatched copies. An equal value increases the balance; a different value cancels one copy. When the balance empties, the next value begins a new candidate group.
majority-element.observation: Change the candidate only at zero balance; the strict-majority guarantee is essential.
approach: Start a candidate group when no unmatched votes remain.
Add a matching vote or cancel a differing vote.
Return the surviving candidate.
majority-element.correctness: Removing a pair of different values can remove at most one occurrence of a strict majority. Since its original count exceeds all other counts combined, it cannot be canceled completely. The balance process performs exactly such pair cancellation, leaving its final candidate equal to that majority.
majority-element.cost: One vote update per value gives linear work. The candidate and balance use constant extra memory.
pitfalls: Change the candidate only at zero balance; the strict-majority guarantee is essential.
Cancellation alone does not prove a majority in arbitrary input.

house-robber.question: Which two earlier street totals are enough to decide about the next house?
intuition: Taking the largest visible house greedily can block two houses whose combined amount is larger. Enumerating every legal selection revisits the same prefix-street question.

At each house, compare skipping it with taking it. Skipping keeps the previous prefix’s best total. Taking it adds its money to the best total ending before its immediate neighbor. Only those two earlier best totals are needed.
house-robber.observation: Taking a house excludes its immediate predecessor; skipping it retains the previous best total.
approach: Remember the best totals for the two preceding street prefixes.
Compare skipping this house with taking it plus the older prefix best.
Advance both saved prefix totals together.
house-robber.correctness: Any legal selection of a prefix either skips its last house or takes it. In the first case its best total is the preceding prefix’s best. In the second, it must skip the preceding neighbor and can add the current amount to the best older prefix. These exhaustive possibilities justify the maximum at every house.
house-robber.cost: Compute two candidate totals per house. A few rolling prefix totals provide linear work and constant auxiliary memory.
pitfalls: Taking a house excludes its immediate predecessor; skipping it retains the previous best total.
Do not assume alternating houses always maximizes money.

binary-tree-right-side-view.question: Why can a visible rightmost node belong to a left subtree?
intuition: Following only right-child links fails when the right subtree ends before a deeper left subtree. Visibility depends on the rightmost existing node at each depth.
Collect a whole level in left-to-right queue order. Its last node is the one visible from the right. Repeat at every depth, even after right-side branches disappear.

approach: Process one depth level at a time.
Keep child queue order left to right.
Record the last value of each level.
binary-tree-right-side-view.correctness: Breadth-first grouping lists all existing nodes at each depth left to right. Looking from the right hides every earlier node behind the last existing one. Recording precisely that node per level therefore gives the complete right-side view, independent of which subtree it belongs to.

pitfalls: Take the last existing node of each complete level, not merely the next right child.

number-of-islands.question: How does painting a whole connected patch count it only once?
intuition: Counting individual land squares overcounts islands. Even starting a separate traversal at every land square would recount patches that were already discovered.

When the scan finds unvisited land, count one new island and flood through all side-connected land from it. Mark the whole patch before scanning onward. Later squares in that patch are already accounted for.
number-of-islands.observation: Only shared sides connect land; diagonal contact does not join islands.
approach: Scan for an unvisited land square.
Count one island and mark all side-connected land in its flood.
Continue until every land square belongs to a counted flood.
number-of-islands.correctness: A flood reaches exactly the land connected to its starting square by side-sharing paths. Marking that component prevents any of its cells from starting another count. Every component contains a first unvisited cell in the scan, which starts one flood. Thus components and counted islands correspond one to one.
number-of-islands.cost: Each cell is scanned and each land square is flooded at most once, so work grows with grid area. The flood frontier can hold a grid-sized number of cells.
pitfalls: Only shared sides connect land; diagonal contact does not join islands.
Use four-direction adjacency, not diagonal adjacency.

remove-linked-list-elements.question: How can one predecessor bookmark remove even several adjacent unwanted nodes?
intuition: Deleting the current node without its predecessor makes head deletion and consecutive deletions awkward. The incoming link is what must change.

Add a temporary starting node before the head. Inspect the node after the predecessor bookmark. If it is unwanted, bypass it while keeping the predecessor fixed; otherwise advance to that retained node.

approach: Place a temporary node before the head.
Bypass unwanted successors, keeping the predecessor fixed.
Advance only when retaining a successor, then return the first real node.
remove-linked-list-elements.correctness: The predecessor’s completed prefix contains exactly the retained original nodes in order. Bypassing an unwanted successor extends inspection without adding it; advancing over a wanted successor extends the retained prefix. Repeating these actions examines every node and leaves exactly the desired chain.
remove-linked-list-elements.cost: Every node is inspected once. One temporary node and a bookmark use constant extra memory; work is linear.
pitfalls: After a removal, stay at the predecessor and inspect its new successor.
Return the temporary start’s final successor.

course-schedule.question: How does removing finished prerequisites reveal the next ready courses?
intuition: Following prerequisites recursively can revisit the same requirements. The key question for each course is how many prerequisites are still unfinished.

Begin with courses that have no remaining requirements. Finishing one removes a requirement from each dependent course. A course becomes ready only when all its requirements have been removed. A directed cycle keeps its members waiting forever.
course-schedule.observation: A dependent course becomes ready only when its remaining prerequisite count reaches zero.
approach: Count unfinished prerequisites for each course.
Take ready courses and remove their outgoing requirement obligations.
Return the completed order if requested, or whether all courses finish; a stalled incomplete process means a cycle.
course-schedule.correctness: Each ready course has no unfinished prerequisites, so taking it respects all its constraints. Removing its requirements preserves the exact unfinished counts. implement-trie-prefix-tree.question: Why is following a letter path different from finding a whole stored word?
intuition: Independent word storage repeats shared beginnings. But combining beginnings also creates a subtle distinction: a path can exist without its prefix having been inserted as a complete word.

Store letters as edges from a shared root. Words sharing a prefix reuse those edges. Mark complete-word endpoints separately. Prefix queries need only an existing path; whole-word queries also need its endpoint marker.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.observation: An existing path proves a prefix; only an end marker proves a whole inserted word.
approach: Insert each letter along a shared path and mark its endpoint.
For a prefix query, require the full path.
For a word query, require the path and its end marker.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.correctness: Every inserted word follows its exact sequence of letter edges and marks its final node. A query follows those same edges, so a missing edge rules out that prefix. At the final node, the marker records precisely whether that full word was inserted. Shared prefix edges preserve all longer words without implying extra shorter words.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.cost: Each operation follows at most one edge per letter, giving linear work in query or word length. Stored nodes grow with distinct prefix characters across all inserted words.
pitfalls: An existing path proves a prefix; only an end marker proves a whole inserted word.
The same path can answer both queries yes when it has an endpoint marker.

intuition: Trying every continuous section repeatedly sums the same values. A running framed sum can be updated by adding or removing one endpoint.

intuition: Searching the board separately for each word repeats common prefix walks. A board route that is no prefix of any requested word cannot lead to an answer.

Build a shared letter-prefix tree for the requested words. Walk adjacent board squares while following that tree. Stop when no matching prefix edge exists. A complete-word marker reports a match, and removing only that marker prevents duplicate reports while preserving longer continuations.

intuition: The line-street rule overlooks that the first and last houses are neighbors in a circle. A line answer selecting both endpoints can therefore be invalid.

invert-binary-tree.question: What happens when every left turn becomes a right turn?
intuition: Mirroring just the root exchanges two big subtrees but does not mirror the structures inside them. Every node’s local left-right choice must be reversed.
Visit each original node and exchange its two child links. Apply the same operation inside both descendants. Values remain attached to their original nodes; only directions change.

Continue through both children.
Return the same root of the now-mirrored tree.
invert-binary-tree.correctness: Each original root-to-node path is a sequence of left and right directions. Swapping links at every ancestor replaces each direction with its opposite, placing that same node at its mirror position. Visiting every node performs the complete reflection without changing values or creating nodes.
invert-binary-tree.cost: Visit each node once. Depth-first pending visits use memory proportional to tree height in the worst case.
pitfalls: Swap child links at every node, not merely at the root.
Missing children exchange just like real child links.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.question: Why does left-node-right visitation reveal rank directly?
intuition: Collecting and sorting all tree values ignores the binary search tree’s ordering. We only need to visit enough values to reach the requested rank.

A left subtree contains smaller values, then comes the node, then its larger right subtree. Follow the leftmost unfinished path, visit its next node, and move into that node’s right subtree. This produces ascending values directly.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.observation: Count actual node visits in inorder, stopping at the requested rank.
approach: Save the leftmost unfinished ancestor chain.
Visit its next node and count it in ascending order.
Continue into the right subtree, stopping at the requested visit.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.correctness: The search-tree ordering puts every left-subtree value before its node and every right-subtree value after it. Inorder visitation therefore lists all values in ascending order. The explicit ancestor stack preserves that visit order, so the requested numbered visit equals the requested smallest rank.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.cost: Descend at most tree height initially, then perform the needed visits; worst-case work is linear in node count. The ancestor stack uses height-sized memory.
pitfalls: Count actual node visits in inorder, stopping at the requested rank.
Do not use root depth as value rank.

range-sum-query-immutable.question: How can two totals answer the sum of any requested section?
intuition: Adding every requested section repeats work whenever queries overlap. Since the numbers never change, the sum before each boundary can be calculated once.

Place a cumulative total at every gap between numbers, including zero before the first number. A section’s sum is its ending boundary total minus its starting boundary total: everything before the section cancels.

approach: Build cumulative totals from left to right.

Subtract the earlier total from the later.
range-sum-query-immutable.correctness: Each saved boundary total equals the sum of all preceding values, by induction while building it. Subtracting the total preceding a section from the total through its last value removes precisely the values outside its left boundary and retains every requested value once.
range-sum-query-immutable.cost: Building the boundary totals takes one pass and linear storage. Every later section query uses two lookups and one subtraction, regardless of its length.
pitfalls: Use totals at the two outside boundaries of the requested section.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.question: How can yesterday’s sale prevent today’s tempting purchase?
intuition: Greedily collecting every price increase can buy again immediately after a sale, breaking the one-day cooldown. Future choices depend on whether a share is held and whether yesterday ended in a sale.

Keep three best daily outcomes: holding a share, selling today, and resting without a share. A new purchase may use only yesterday’s resting outcome. A sale uses yesterday’s holding outcome; resting can follow rest or a completed cooldown.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.observation: Compare transitions from the preceding day before replacing any daily outcomes.
approach: Start with zero money while resting and no possible holding or sale outcome.
Evaluate holding, selling, and resting for each price from the preceding day’s outcomes.
Finish with the better outcome that holds no share.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.correctness: Every valid daily history ends in exactly one of holding, selling today, or resting without a share. Its preceding state must be one of the allowed transitions. Choosing the best predecessor for each state therefore captures every legal history while excluding a purchase immediately following a sale.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.cost: A constant number of daily outcomes is updated once per price, giving linear time and constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Compare transitions from the preceding day before replacing any daily outcomes.
Do not treat a held share’s accounting total as completed profit.

minimum-height-trees.question: Why do the centers of a tree survive peeling its outer leaves?
intuition: Trying every root and measuring its farthest distance repeats long traversals. A tree’s longest paths are bounded by outer leaves, so choosing a root closer to their middle reduces the worst distance.

Remove all current leaves together, then repeat on the smaller tree. Peeling trims both ends of every longest path equally. The final one or two nodes are its centers and give the smallest possible rooted height.
minimum-height-trees.observation: Peel an entire leaf layer simultaneously; stop when at most two nodes remain.
approach: Count every node’s remaining neighbors.
Remove a complete layer of degree-one leaves and update neighboring degrees.
Return the final one or two centers.
minimum-height-trees.correctness: A farthest vertex from a tree root is a leaf. Removing all leaves shortens the competing longest routes from both ends without changing which surviving vertices minimize maximum distance. Repeating this symmetric reduction leaves the middle vertex or middle pair of a diameter, the only possible minimum-height roots.
minimum-height-trees.cost: Each node enters a leaf layer once and each edge is removed once. Neighbor lists, degrees, and layer queues use linear time and storage.
pitfalls: Peel an entire leaf layer simultaneously; stop when at most two nodes remain.
The input must be a connected acyclic tree.

generalized-abbreviation.question: How can an omitted run be remembered without writing one marker per letter?
intuition: Choosing whether to keep each letter produces all possibilities, but writing a separate 1 for every omitted letter would create ambiguous or noncanonical adjacent counts.
Walk along the word with a count of consecutive omitted letters. Omitting extends that run; keeping a letter first writes the pending count, then the letter. At the end, write any remaining run once.
generalized-abbreviation.observation: An omission count represents one consecutive run, and is flushed before the next kept letter.
approach: Branch at each letter: omit it or keep it.
Accumulate consecutive omissions into one count.
Flush that count before a kept letter or at the word’s end.
generalized-abbreviation.correctness: Every subset of kept positions determines one branch path and one abbreviation. Consecutive omitted positions are represented by their exact run length, while kept letters separate runs. This gives every valid abbreviation and prevents two branch paths from producing the same canonical pattern.
generalized-abbreviation.cost: There are two choices at each of the word’s positions, so output is exponential. Writing each abbreviation takes up to the word length; the recursive choice path is linear in depth, with additional copying work for constructed prefixes.
pitfalls: An omission count represents one consecutive run, and is flushed before the next kept letter.
Flush a final omitted run even when no letter follows.
generalized-abbreviation.artAlt: Neighboring omission capsules merge into one longer run between retained letter tiles.
generalized-abbreviation.artCaption: Consecutive omitted letters belong to one count. Keeping a letter closes that run and starts a new choice.

number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.question: How can one exploration identify a whole connected component?
intuition: Testing every pair of vertices for connectivity repeats the same routes. Once an exploration reaches all vertices connected to one starting vertex, they form a complete component.
Choose any still-unvisited vertex and follow all its connections until no new vertex is reachable. Mark that whole group, count one component, then start again from another unvisited vertex.
number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.observation: Start a new component only from a vertex no earlier exploration reached.
approach: Build neighbor lists for all vertices, including isolated ones.
Explore every newly found vertex’s neighbors and mark discoveries.
Count one component per exploration started from an unvisited vertex.
number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.correctness: Following all neighbors reaches every vertex connected to the start, and never crosses into a disconnected group because no connecting route exists. Starting again only at unseen vertices produces disjoint exhaustive groups, so the number of starts equals the number of connected components.
number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.cost: Each vertex is discovered once and each undirected edge is examined from both ends. Work and neighbor-list storage are proportional to vertices plus edges.
pitfalls: Start a new component only from a vertex no earlier exploration reached.
Do not omit vertices just because they have no edge.

count-of-range-sum.question: How can sorted prefix totals count section sums without losing section order?
intuition: Listing every continuous section takes quadratic work. A section sum is the difference between two prefix totals, but the earlier boundary must stay earlier in the original sequence.

Split prefix boundaries by their original positions. Recursively count pairs inside each half; for pairs crossing halves, the first boundary must be in the earlier half. Sorted totals then allow two moving boundaries to count differences inside the requested sum band.
count-of-range-sum.observation: Separate earlier and later boundary positions before sorting their totals.
approach: Build cumulative totals with an initial zero.
Recursively count qualifying pairs within each positional half.
Count crossing pairs using a lower-inclusive and upper-inclusive band, then merge sorted totals.
count-of-range-sum.correctness: Each boundary pair either lies inside one half or crosses from the earlier half to the later half, so recursive counting partitions all candidates without overlap. For a fixed earlier total, qualifying later totals lie in one sorted interval determined by the inclusive sum bounds. Moving its two endpoints counts exactly those crossing pairs.
count-of-range-sum.cost: At every split level, sorted-band counting and merging scan a linear number of totals. There are logarithmically many levels, giving linearithmic time and linear extra storage.
pitfalls: Separate earlier and later boundary positions before sorting their totals.
The upper endpoint of the requested sum band is inclusive.

odd-even-linked-list.question: Can the odd-position nodes and even-position nodes be threaded into separate chains?
intuition: Reordering by copying values would replace the original nodes. We need to move links while keeping the order within both position groups, and position parity is different from value parity.

Maintain one chain of odd-position nodes and one of even-position nodes. Reconnect each chain to its next node two positions ahead, preserving a saved start of the even chain. Finally join the odd tail to that saved even start.
odd-even-linked-list.observation: Group by original positions starting at one, while preserving relative order within each group.
approach: Save the first even-position node.
Extend the odd and even chains together through alternating original nodes.
Attach the completed odd tail to the saved even head.
odd-even-linked-list.correctness: Each extension appends the next original odd node to the odd chain and the next original even node to the even chain. Thus both chains keep their original relative orders and contain every node of their position group once. Joining their tails yields exactly the required partition without creating or dropping nodes.
odd-even-linked-list.cost: Each node’s links are handled a constant number of times. Only a few saved node references are needed, giving linear time and constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Group by original positions starting at one, while preserving relative order within each group.
Parity concerns position, not whether the stored number is odd.

counting-bits.question: How can a number reuse the bit count of a smaller number?
intuition: Independently counting all bits of every number repeats overlapping binary prefixes. Removing the final binary digit produces a smaller number whose answer has already been computed.
The number of ones equals the count after dropping the final binary digit, plus one if that removed digit was a one. Build the answers in increasing numeric order, beginning with zero.
counting-bits.observation: Reuse the halved number’s answer, then add the final binary digit.
approach: Give zero a count of zero.
For each positive number, drop its last binary digit.
Add that digit to the already known count for the remaining prefix.
counting-bits.correctness: Zero supplies the base case. Every positive representation splits into a smaller prefix and one last bit. The already-correct prefix count plus that bit is exactly its total one count. Increasing numeric order guarantees the reused answer exists before it is needed.
counting-bits.cost: One constant-size update per number produces a linear-size output. The output is the only growing table; auxiliary storage is constant.
pitfalls: Reuse the halved number’s answer, then add the final binary digit.
The result includes both endpoints, including zero.

intuition: Sorting every value by its frequency spends logarithmic work even though frequencies are bounded between one and the number of input occurrences.

Count each distinct value, then place it in the bucket named by its count. Visit buckets from largest count downward until enough values have been collected. Numeric value order has no role in frequency ranking.
top-k-frequent-elements.observation: Select by frequency, stopping after the requested number of distinct values.
approach: Count every occurrence of each value.
Place distinct values in buckets indexed by their occurrence count.
Read buckets from high frequency to low until the requested count is reached.
top-k-frequent-elements.correctness: Counting places every distinct value into exactly its frequency bucket. Descending bucket order therefore visits values in nonincreasing frequency order. Taking the first requested number yields the most frequent distinct values; within a tied bucket any accepted tie order is valid.
top-k-frequent-elements.cost: Counting and bucket construction take linear work; scanning the bounded frequency levels is also linear. Counts, buckets, and selected results use linear total storage.
pitfalls: Select by frequency, stopping after the requested number of distinct values.
Do not return repeated copies of a frequent value.

rearrange-string-k-distance-apart.question: How does a cooldown queue make repeated letters safe to reuse?
intuition: Selecting the most frequent letter at every position can repeat it too soon. We need both remaining supply and the earliest position at which a recently used letter becomes eligible again.

Among eligible letters, choose one with the most copies remaining. Temporarily remove it from the available choices and record its release position. A cooldown queue returns letters only when their required spacing has elapsed.
rearrange-string-k-distance-apart.observation: A letter used at position p is unavailable until position p plus the required distance.
approach: Count remaining copies and organize currently eligible letters by remaining frequency.
At each output position, release letters whose cooldown has ended.
Choose the most frequent eligible letter, then cool it down if copies remain.
rearrange-string-k-distance-apart.correctness: The cooldown rule ensures every chosen letter respects its separation from its last occurrence. Choosing the largest eligible remaining supply avoids unnecessarily postponing the hardest demand; an exchange argument can move such a choice earlier in a feasible schedule without worsening the spacing of the displaced smaller demand. If no letter is eligible while output remains, the current position cannot be filled under the remaining cooldown requirements.
rearrange-string-k-distance-apart.cost: Each character placement uses bounded queue work and a priority operation over distinct letters. Time is proportional to output length times the logarithm of distinct-letter count; count and cooldown records scale with the alphabet.
pitfalls: A letter used at position p is unavailable until position p plus the required distance.
Do not add idle placeholders: every output position must be an original letter.

find-k-pairs-with-smallest-sums.question: Why is each first-array value the head of an ordered row of pairs?
intuition: Forming all pairs wastes work when only a few smallest sums are requested. With sorted arrays, pairing one fixed first value with successive second values creates an ascending row of sums.
Keep only the next unseen pair from each relevant row. Select the smallest row head, output it, and advance that row by one. The row heads collectively represent the smallest pair not yet returned.
find-k-pairs-with-smallest-sums.observation: After removing a row head, expose only the next pair in that same row.
approach: Start a row at the first second-array value for the first few first-array values.
Compare the exposed row heads by pair sum.
Output the smallest head and advance its row until enough pairs are returned.
find-k-pairs-with-smallest-sums.correctness: Each row is sorted, so its head is its smallest unreturned pair. The minimum among all exposed heads is consequently the global smallest unreturned pair. Advancing only that row restores the invariant. Rows beyond the first requested-count first values cannot be needed earlier, since that many initial row heads already have sums no larger than their first head.
find-k-pairs-with-smallest-sums.cost: The frontier contains at most the smaller of first-array length and requested count. Each returned pair uses a logarithmic frontier update; extra frontier storage matches that bound, in addition to the output.
pitfalls: After removing a row head, expose only the next pair in that same row.
Equal values at separate positions still represent separate pairs.

combination-sum-iv.question: Why do different last choices count different ordered constructions?
intuition: Enumerating every ordered sequence repeatedly solves the same remaining-total questions. Unlike unordered coin selection, 1 then 2 and 2 then 1 are different constructions.

Count ordered constructions of every total. Every nonempty construction has one last value, and removing it leaves a construction of a smaller total. Add those smaller counts over all allowed last values.
combination-sum-iv.observation: An empty construction supplies one way to make total zero.
approach: Start total zero with one empty construction.
For each increasing positive total, consider every allowed final value that fits.
Add the counts for the corresponding smaller totals.
combination-sum-iv.correctness: Every ordered construction has exactly one final value. Removing it maps that construction to exactly one counted smaller construction, and appending it reverses the mapping. These disjoint exhaustive final-value groups justify the sum. Positive choices ensure all reused totals are smaller, so increasing total order supplies correct counts.
combination-sum-iv.cost: For each total through the target, inspect every allowed value. Work scales as target times choice count; a table through the target uses linear target-sized storage.
pitfalls: An empty construction supplies one way to make total zero.
Do not reorder the loops as though counting unordered combinations.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.question: How can counting entries below a trial value replace extracting them one by one?
intuition: Flattening and sorting the matrix ignores its already sorted rows and columns. Instead, ask how many entries are no greater than a proposed answer value.

For a trial value, walk a staircase from the bottom-left corner. If an entry qualifies, every entry above it in that column qualifies; count them and move right. Otherwise move up. Binary search the smallest value whose count reaches the requested rank.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.observation: Search for the first value with at least the requested number of entries at or below it.
approach: Bound the answer by the smallest and largest matrix entries.
Count entries at or below a trial using sorted rows and columns.
Narrow the value range until the first qualifying value remains.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.correctness: Column and row sortedness makes the staircase count exact: a qualifying bottom entry certifies all entries above, while an oversized entry excludes its row position and everything below there. The count is nondecreasing in the trial value. Binary search therefore finds the first threshold whose count reaches the rank, precisely the value occupying that sorted rank.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.cost: Each count visits at most one linear staircase through rows and columns. Binary search makes logarithmically many trials in the numeric value range. The counting walk uses constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Search for the first value with at least the requested number of entries at or below it.
Count duplicate entries separately.

is-subsequence.question: Why is the earliest available matching character always safe?
intuition: Trying every way to delete letters from the longer text would enumerate many redundant choices. We only need to preserve the query’s order, not adjacency.

Scan the longer text from left to right, waiting for the next required query character. Accept its first available match. Earlier matching positions leave at least as much remaining text as any later alternative.
is-subsequence.observation: Advance the query only when its next needed character is found.
approach: Begin waiting for the first query character.
Scan the text, accepting each next required character at its earliest occurrence.
Succeed when all query characters have matched in order.
is-subsequence.correctness: Suppose any valid matching sequence exists. Its first required character cannot occur earlier than the greedy first match. Replacing its first position with that greedy position leaves the remaining matches feasible. Repeating this argument for every query character proves earliest matching succeeds whenever any match exists.
is-subsequence.cost: The text is scanned once and the query progresses only forward. Time is linear in the text length, with constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Advance the query only when its next needed character is found.
Equal letters must match separate successive positions.

partition-equal-subset-sum.question: How does reaching half the total settle the whole partition?
intuition: Enumerating both subsets duplicates the same decision: once one subset is chosen, the other consists of everything left. Equal totals require one subset to reach half the overall total.

If the total is even, track reachable subset sums through its half. Each value can extend sums reachable before that value was used. Update from larger sums downward so one occurrence cannot extend itself repeatedly.
partition-equal-subset-sum.observation: Each input occurrence may be used at most once; new sums must extend older reachability.
approach: Reject an odd overall total.

pacific-atlantic-water-flow.question: What happens if we trace possible water routes backward from each ocean?
intuition: Starting downhill searches independently from every cell revisits the same routes. It is easier to ask which cells can reach one ocean by reversing the direction of a valid flow.

Begin at each ocean’s bordering cells and explore inland only to equally high or higher neighbors. Those reversed routes identify every cell that can flow downhill to that ocean. Intersect the two reached sets.

Explore uphill from the bottom and right borders for the second ocean.
Return cells reached from both ocean borders.

A cell reached from an ocean border therefore has a valid forward route back to that ocean, and every such route can be followed backward. The intersection is exactly the cells with routes to both oceans.

pitfalls: A reversed step climbs or stays level; the corresponding forward water step descends or stays level.

palindrome-linked-list.question: Can reversing only the back half make mirrored nodes walkable together?
intuition: A singly linked list cannot compare its front and back by walking backward. Copying all values would solve that, but needs growing memory.

Find the middle and reverse the second half. Its forward order now matches the original list’s backward order. Compare the two half chains node by node, skipping an odd middle node. Reverse the changed half again before returning.
palindrome-linked-list.observation: Compare mirrored values, then restore the reversed half even if a mismatch is found.
approach: Find the middle and start of the comparison half.
Reverse that half and compare it with the front half.
Restore its original links before returning the comparison result.
palindrome-linked-list.correctness: Reversing the second half puts its original last node opposite the first, its next-to-last opposite the second, and so on. Comparing every such pair establishes exactly the palindrome condition. An odd middle is its own mirror. Restoring the half returns all original links independently of the result.
palindrome-linked-list.cost: Middle finding, half reversal, comparison, and restoration are each linear passes. A few bookmarks give constant auxiliary memory.
pitfalls: Compare mirrored values, then restore the reversed half even if a mismatch is found.
Restoration is also required after an early mismatch.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.question: Where do the ordered search routes to two nodes first split?
intuition: Searching the whole tree ignores its value ordering. If both targets lie on the same side of a node, their lowest shared ancestor must also be on that side.

Follow both target values together. Move left when both are smaller and right when both are larger. Stop at their first split, or when the current node is itself a target. That is the lowest shared ancestor.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.observation: Continue only while both targets lie strictly on the same ordered side.
approach: Compare both target values with the current node.
Move into their shared side when both agree.
Return the first split or target node.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.correctness: At a node where both targets lie on one side, all other positions can be excluded by search-tree ordering, and their lowest common ancestor remains in that shared subtree. At the first split, both targets descend from the current node but no child contains both. If the current node is a target, it is itself the lowest ancestor containing both. Hence the stop is exact.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.cost: Follow one root-to-node path, so work is proportional to tree height. No ancestor collection is required; extra memory is constant.
pitfalls: Continue only while both targets lie strictly on the same ordered side.
A node counts as its own ancestor.

product-of-array-except-self.question: Can left and right products exclude a value without division?
intuition: Dividing a full product by each value fails at zero and may violate the operation restriction. Recomputing every omitted-value product repeats multiplication.

For each position, all other values divide into a left group and a right group. Store the left product in the output during a forward pass. During a backward pass, multiply it by the current right product before adding the current value to that product.

approach: Write the product of earlier values at each position.
Walk backward, multiplying by the product of later values.
Advance the right product after updating the current output.
product-of-array-except-self.correctness: At each position, the forward saved product contains exactly earlier values, and the backward running product contains exactly later values. Their product contains every other input value once and the current value zero times. Multiplication therefore gives each required output without division, even when zeros occur.
product-of-array-except-self.cost: Two passes perform linear multiplication work. Beyond the required output, only two running products use constant auxiliary memory.
pitfalls: Store the product before including the current value on each pass.
Zero requires no division-specific repair.

sliding-window-maximum.question: Why can a newer larger value erase an older smaller maximum candidate?
intuition: Scanning every window repeats maximum comparisons. Not every current value deserves to remain a future candidate.

Keep candidate positions in a queue with decreasing values. A newer value at least as large as an older candidate dominates it: it is better now and will expire later. Remove expired front positions, and read the maximum from the remaining front.
sliding-window-maximum.observation: An older candidate no larger than a newer one can be removed permanently.
approach: Remove candidates that have left the current window.
Remove weaker candidates from the back before adding the new position.
Read the front candidate once the window is complete.
sliding-window-maximum.correctness: Every removed weaker candidate has a newer replacement at least as large, so it cannot become maximum before that replacement expires. Expired candidates cannot influence the current window. The decreasing queue therefore retains a valid dominating representative for every discarded active value, and its front is the window maximum.
sliding-window-maximum.cost: Each position enters once and leaves at most once from either end. Work is linear; candidate memory is bounded by the window width, plus output.
pitfalls: An older candidate no larger than a newer one can be removed permanently.

intuition: Checking every pair of meetings repeats overlap work. Once starts are sorted, a schedule can be checked at its consecutive boundaries.

Sort meetings by start time. Compare each start with its predecessor’s end. Starting exactly when the predecessor ends is allowed: these time spans are half-open, so the shared endpoint is not occupied twice.

approach: Sort by meeting start.
Reject a meeting beginning before its predecessor ends.
Accept after all consecutive boundaries fit.
meeting-rooms.correctness: If every sorted adjacent pair fits, each earlier meeting ends before the next begins, and chaining these boundaries separates all earlier and later meetings. meeting-rooms-ii.question: How does the busiest moment determine the number of rooms?
intuition: A total meeting count ignores room reuse. What matters is how many meetings are active simultaneously.

Process starts chronologically and keep active meeting ends in a minimum-priority queue. Before a new meeting begins, release every meeting whose end has arrived. Add the new end and remember the greatest active count.

approach: Sort meetings by start time.
Remove ended meetings from the active-end queue.
Add the new meeting and remember the peak active count.
meeting-rooms-ii.correctness: At each start, removing ended meetings leaves exactly those overlapping the new meeting. Their count plus the new one is the simultaneous demand. No schedule can use fewer than the peak demand. Reusing released rooms realizes that demand without extra rooms, so the maximum active count is sufficient and necessary.

pitfalls: Release all ends at or before the next start; equal endpoints can reuse a room.
Use an end-at-or-before-start release test.

factor-combinations.question: How do increasing factors avoid reordered copies of the same product?
intuition: Trying factors in arbitrary order repeats collections such as 2×6 and 6×2. A number also may be broken into more than two factors.

Try a divisor no smaller than the previous factor. Pair it with the remaining quotient for one answer, then explore splitting that quotient further. Only divisors through its square root need to be tried; the larger counterpart is already the quotient.
factor-combinations.observation: Use factors greater than one in nondecreasing order, and split the remaining quotient further when possible.
approach: Try increasing divisors of the remaining product.
Save the chosen prefix plus a divisor and its quotient.
Continue splitting the quotient with no smaller future factors.
factor-combinations.correctness: Every nontrivial factor collection can be sorted into nondecreasing order. Its next smallest factor divides the remaining product and is no greater than the square root when at least two factors remain. The search tries that factor and can continue along the collection. Saving quotients covers final pairs, while increasing-order constraints prevent reordered duplicates.

pitfalls: Use factors greater than one in nondecreasing order, and split the remaining quotient further when possible.

binary-tree-paths.question: How can a branch carry its route without leaking into its sibling?
intuition: Saving a path at every node would include incomplete root-to-node routes. Keeping a shared history without undoing also mixes one branch’s values into another.
Append each visited node to the current route. At a leaf, save its joined value sequence. On returning, remove the current value so another branch begins with exactly the shared ancestors.
binary-tree-paths.observation: Save routes only at leaves, and undo the current node when returning.
approach: Append the current node to the route.
Save its complete route if it is a leaf, otherwise visit children.
Remove the current node before returning to the parent.
binary-tree-paths.correctness: The active route contains exactly the current node’s root ancestors because values are appended on entry and removed on return. Saving at leaves therefore emits complete root-to-leaf routes. Traversing both children reaches every leaf, and undoing prevents sibling-route contamination.
binary-tree-paths.cost: Each node is entered and left once. Writing path strings adds work proportional to their total output length. The active route uses height-sized memory.
pitfalls: Save routes only at leaves, and undo the current node when returning.
Do not require at least one child edge to save a path.

graph-valid-tree.question: Why do connectivity and one-fewer edges certify an undirected tree?
intuition: Checking only reachability can accept a connected graph with cycles. Checking only the edge count can accept a disconnected graph whose cycle uses extra edges elsewhere.

An undirected tree with all vertices has exactly one fewer edge than vertices. Check that count, then traverse from one vertex and verify all are reachable. These two conditions together force the connected structure to have no cycle.

Traverse undirected neighbors from a starting vertex.

graph-valid-tree.correctness: A connected undirected graph needs at least one fewer edge than vertices to connect them all. If it had a cycle, one cycle edge could be removed while preserving connectivity, contradicting that minimum count. Therefore full connectivity with exactly that count implies an acyclic connected graph, precisely a tree.

pitfalls: Require both full connectivity and exactly one fewer edge than vertices.
Do not reject the one-vertex zero-edge case.

alien-dictionary.question: What can the first differing letters of neighboring words tell us about an unknown alphabet?
intuition: Later differing letters do not impose independent ordering rules: lexical comparison is decided at the first mismatch. A longer word before its exact shorter prefix is impossible under any alphabet.

Compare adjacent words and create a directed rule from each first mismatching letter to the other. Then repeatedly emit a letter with no unmet earlier-letter rules. Include all observed letters, even those with no rule.
alien-dictionary.observation: Use only the first mismatch, reject reversed prefix order, and detect cycles in the letter rules.
approach: Create vertices for every observed letter.
Extract the first-mismatch rule for each adjacent word pair.
Emit letters with no unmet rules; reject a cycle or impossible prefix order.
alien-dictionary.correctness: An adjacent pair’s first mismatch gives exactly its necessary letter-order rule, while a reversed prefix pair is intrinsically invalid. Any ordering satisfying all those rules orders the entire adjacent-word chain correctly. Removing ready letters constructs such an ordering; if a cycle stalls it, no consistent alphabet can satisfy the contradictory rules.
alien-dictionary.cost: Read word characters for comparisons and process each unique letter rule once. Work is linear in total characters plus letter vertices and rule edges; graph storage follows vertices and edges.
pitfalls: Use only the first mismatch, reject reversed prefix order, and detect cycles in the letter rules.
A prefix error is not repaired by adding letter arrows.

move-zeroes.question: How can a write frontier preserve nonzero order while zeros collect behind it?
intuition: Repeatedly deleting zeros and shifting the row wastes movement. Sorting zeros away might also reorder nonzero values, violating stability.

Keep a frontier marking the next slot for a nonzero value. Read left to right. Each nonzero exchanges into that frontier and advances it; a zero leaves it unchanged. The completed prefix follows original nonzero order.
move-zeroes.observation: Advance the write frontier only after placing a nonzero value.
approach: Read values in original order.
Exchange each nonzero into the next prefix slot.
Leave zeros behind and return the changed original row.
move-zeroes.correctness: After each read, the prefix contains exactly the nonzero values encountered, in encounter order. Swapping the next nonzero into the frontier extends that invariant. Any displaced prefix-gap value is zero. At the end all nonzeros occupy the prefix and all remaining positions contain zeros, with no nonzero reordered.
move-zeroes.cost: Read each value once and perform at most one exchange per nonzero. Work is linear and auxiliary memory constant.
pitfalls: Advance the write frontier only after placing a nonzero value.
A zero is a value to move back, not a signal to stop reading.

find-the-duplicate-number.question: Why does reading values as next addresses turn a duplicate into a cycle entrance?
intuition: A membership table needs extra memory, and altering values is forbidden. The bounded positive values let the row describe a next-address structure without changing it.

Treat each value as the address to visit next, starting at address zero. Since zero is never a stored target, the route enters a loop from outside it. The repeated value identifies the entrance with multiple incoming routes. Use slow-fast detection, then equal-speed entrance finding.
find-the-duplicate-number.observation: Follow addresses without changing values; return the cycle entrance value.
approach: Follow one-link and two-link address walkers until they meet.
Restart one walker at address zero.
Move both one link until they meet again at the entrance.
find-the-duplicate-number.correctness: The bounded address map forces the route to repeat. Starting from zero enters its eventual cycle through a value receiving repeated incoming references; under the unique-duplicate promise that entrance is the repeated value. Slow-fast movement detects the cycle, and the cycle-distance relation makes equal-speed walkers from zero and the meeting align at its entrance.
find-the-duplicate-number.cost: Both address-walking phases traverse a linear number of links. A few address bookmarks use constant memory and leave the input unchanged.
pitfalls: Follow addresses without changing values; return the cycle entrance value.
Do not rely on the duplicated occurrence count being exactly two.

intuition: Sorting all received values after each insertion repeats ordering work. Only the two values at the boundary between smaller and larger halves are needed for the median.

intuition: A sequence of real values alone can describe several different shapes. Reconstruction needs to know where a left or right child is missing.

longest-increasing-subsequence.question: Why is a smaller ending value a better representative of the same subsequence length?
intuition: Listing all subsequences grows exponentially. Keeping just one arbitrary subsequence can also discard a more extendable alternative of the same length.

For each achievable length, remember the smallest ending value among increasing subsequences of that length. A smaller ending is easier for a future value to exceed. Find the first ending no smaller than the new value and replace it; append if the new value exceeds every ending.
longest-increasing-subsequence.observation: Replace the first ending at least as large as the new value; equality must not increase a strictly increasing length.
approach: Keep the smallest ending for each attainable length.
Locate the first ending no smaller than the new value.
Replace it or append a new attainable length; return the number of saved lengths.
longest-increasing-subsequence.correctness: A new value can extend any shorter subsequence whose smallest ending is below it. Replacing the first ending no smaller than that value gives the smallest possible ending for the corresponding length without changing longer feasible lengths. Appending occurs exactly when one longer increasing subsequence becomes achievable. The summary length is therefore the maximum increasing length.

longest-repeating-character-replacement.question: How many changes does a section need to become one repeated letter?
intuition: Trying every section and every replacement repeats large counts. In any one section, the best letter to retain is the most frequent one; every other position must change.

Maintain a moving section and its letter counts. Its minimum changes equal section length minus its largest letter count. If this exceeds the budget, remove characters from the left until the section fits again.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.observation: A section qualifies exactly when its length minus its highest letter count is within the replacement budget.
approach: Add the next character to the current section.
Shrink from the left while too many replacements are required.
Record the greatest qualifying length seen.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.correctness: The highest-frequency letter requires the fewest changes, so the validity formula is exact. Removing characters cannot increase the minimum required changes. For each right endpoint, shrinking only invalid left boundaries retains the longest valid section ending there; a discarded invalid boundary cannot become valid by extending farther. pitfalls: A section qualifies exactly when its length minus its highest letter count is within the replacement budget.

word-squares.question: How can the next row be forced by the columns already chosen?
intuition: Trying arbitrary word sequences ignores the square condition until too late. Once earlier rows exist, their letters in the next column already determine the beginning of the next row.
Index words by prefixes. At row depth d, read column d of every chosen row to form the required prefix. Branch only among words with that prefix, and undo the choice after exploring it.
word-squares.observation: The next row must begin with the letters already present in its matching column.
approach: Index each word under all its prefixes.
Build the next required prefix from the chosen rows’ column letters.
Explore matching next words until a complete square is formed.
word-squares.correctness: When a new row is chosen, its required prefix checks every symmetric pair against earlier rows. Later rows will check the remaining pairs. A completed square therefore satisfies every row-column equality. Conversely, every valid square’s next word has exactly the required prefix, so the branching search cannot exclude it.
word-squares.cost: Prefix indexing reduces the candidates at each depth, but the search can still branch exponentially in word length. Index storage includes copied prefixes; the working square has only one word per row, in addition to returned squares.
pitfalls: The next row must begin with the letters already present in its matching column.
Do not require the next word to share a prefix with the preceding word.
