non-overlapping-intervals.question: Why does the earliest finishing interval leave the most room for later ones?
intuition: Deleting intervals based on length or starting time can keep a long blocker. It is simpler to maximize the number kept, then subtract that count from the total.

Sort by finishing time. Keep the next interval only when it starts at or after the last kept finish. An earlier finish leaves every later compatible choice available, so it is the safest next interval to keep.
non-overlapping-intervals.observation: Touching endpoints are compatible; select by earliest finish.
approach: Sort intervals by their right endpoint.
Keep each interval whose start is no earlier than the last kept end.
Return total intervals minus kept intervals.
non-overlapping-intervals.correctness: Replace the first interval of any optimal compatible selection with the earliest-finishing available interval. This replacement ends no later and therefore cannot invalidate later selections. Repeating this exchange after every chosen finish proves the greedy selection keeps the maximum possible count, hence minimizes removals.
non-overlapping-intervals.cost: Sorting dominates with linearithmic time. The scan is linear; the sorted interval collection uses linear additional storage in this implementation.
pitfalls: Touching endpoints are compatible; select by earliest finish.
Do not use the closed-balloon rule where touching endpoints count as overlap.

path-sum-iii.question: How can an ancestor’s cumulative total reveal a path beginning below the root?
intuition: Starting a fresh downward search from every node repeatedly sums shared routes. A root-to-current total already contains every possible downward path ending at the current node, once an earlier prefix is removed.

Along the current ancestor route, remember how often each earlier cumulative total occurs. A path totaling the target ends here whenever an earlier total equals the current total minus the target. Remove a node’s saved total when leaving its branch.
path-sum-iii.observation: Count only earlier totals on the current ancestor route, including the empty prefix.
approach: Begin with one empty-prefix total zero.
At each node, count matching earlier totals before recording the current total.
Explore children, then remove the current total on the way back.
path-sum-iii.correctness: Any downward path ending at a node is uniquely defined by an earlier boundary on its ancestor route. Its sum is the current cumulative total minus the boundary total. Frequency counting records distinct boundaries even when totals coincide. Removing prefixes on branch exit keeps only valid ancestors, so every counted path is valid and every valid path is counted at its endpoint.
path-sum-iii.cost: Each node updates one cumulative total and a few frequency records. Work is linear; the active prefix map and traversal path are bounded by tree height.
pitfalls: Count only earlier totals on the current ancestor route, including the empty prefix.
Check for matching earlier totals before adding the current total, avoiding an empty path.

find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.question: Can each value mark its own address inside the same array?
intuition: A separate set can detect repeats, but all values already lie in the addressable range from one through array length. The array’s signs can store whether a value has been seen.

For value v, inspect position v−1. A negative sign means v was seen earlier; otherwise make that addressed entry negative. Read magnitudes while scanning because earlier markings may have changed signs.
find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.observation: Signs store visits; magnitudes retain the original values.
approach: Read the magnitude of each scanned value.
Use its one-based value as a zero-based address.
Report it if that address is already marked; otherwise mark the address negative.
find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.correctness: After processing a prefix, address v−1 is negative exactly when that prefix contains v. The first occurrence marks it; the second observes the mark and reports v. Magnitudes are preserved, so later scans still recover every original value. Under the at-most-twice promise, each duplicate is reported once.
find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.cost: Each value performs constant work at one existing address, so time is linear and auxiliary storage constant, excluding returned duplicates.
pitfalls: Signs store visits; magnitudes retain the original values.
Do not use a negative marked value directly as an address.

find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.question: Why do unmarked addresses reveal absent values?
intuition: Comparing every value from one through array length against the whole input is quadratic. Each allowed value can instead leave a presence mark at its corresponding address.
Make address v−1 negative for every encountered magnitude v. Repeated values preserve the mark rather than toggling it. Afterward, each still-positive address identifies a value that never appeared.
find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.observation: Presence marks are permanent; repeats must not erase them.
approach: Mark the address belonging to each scanned magnitude.
Keep already marked addresses negative.
Read positive addresses as missing one-based values.
find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.correctness: Marking preserves every original magnitude and makes address v−1 negative exactly when v occurs. concatenated-words.question: How can a word be certified by several shorter dictionary words?
intuition: Trying every split combination repeatedly revisits the same prefix boundaries. A boundary can be reached when a preceding reachable boundary connects to it through a dictionary word.

For each candidate word, mark which prefix lengths can be built from dictionary pieces. Extend reachable boundaries with matching pieces, while excluding a match of the entire candidate as one piece. A reachable final boundary then certifies at least two words.
concatenated-words.observation: The whole candidate alone must never count as its own construction.
approach: Begin with the empty boundary reachable.
Test dictionary pieces between earlier reachable boundaries and later boundaries.
Accept a word when its end is reachable through proper pieces.
concatenated-words.correctness: A reachable boundary means exactly that its prefix is a concatenation of dictionary pieces. Every extension preserves that meaning, and every valid construction supplies such a boundary sequence. Excluding the whole-word single piece ensures a reachable nonempty end uses at least two pieces. Thus the test accepts exactly concatenated words.
concatenated-words.cost: For each candidate, testing all boundary pairs is quadratic in length; copied substring checks can add another length factor. The dictionary and one candidate’s reachability table dominate extra storage.
pitfalls: The whole candidate alone must never count as its own construction.
Do not remove repeated use of an allowed smaller word.

sliding-window-median.question: Which two central values determine a moving section’s median?
intuition: Sorting every section independently discards useful ordering from the preceding section. Keep the smaller and larger halves separately as one value leaves and another arrives.

Maintain a lower half with its greatest value exposed and an upper half with its smallest exposed. Keep active half sizes equal, or lower larger by one. Expired values may be marked for later removal until they reach a visible boundary.

approach: Add entering values to the appropriate ordered half.
Mark outgoing occurrences expired and rebalance active half sizes.
Read one middle boundary or average the two boundaries.
sliding-window-median.correctness: The lower half contains values no greater than the upper half, and their active sizes differ by at most one. Therefore the lower maximum is the odd-width middle, or it and the upper minimum are the even-width central pair. Insertion, expiration, cleaning, and rebalancing preserve these ordering and size conditions for each window.
sliding-window-median.cost: Each occurrence is inserted, moved, and eventually removed a bounded number of times with logarithmic heap work. Delayed deletions can retain entries across the whole scan, so this implementation’s worst-case storage and heap scale are linear in total input length, not only section width.
pitfalls: Balance active sizes, and remove expired boundary values before reading the median.
Delayed deletion may retain hidden expired entries; distinguish stored entries from active sizes.

target-sum.question: How do plus and minus choices merge at the same reachable total?
intuition: Enumerating all sign assignments is exponential. Different partial assignments often reach the same total and have identical choices left, so their counts can be combined.

Keep a count of assignments reaching each current total. For the next number, every old assignment creates one new total by adding it and one by subtracting it. Add contributions whenever totals coincide.

approach: Begin with one assignment reaching total zero.
Send each current count to both plus and minus next totals.
After all numbers, read the target’s count or zero.
target-sum.correctness: After each stage, a recorded count equals the number of sign assignments for the processed prefix reaching that total. Each assignment has exactly two extensions, and its last sign uniquely determines which extension created it. Summing all predecessor contributions therefore counts every new assignment exactly once.
target-sum.cost: At each number, process only currently reachable totals. The absolute total is bounded by the sum of magnitudes; time scales with number count times that reachable range, and storage with the range.
pitfalls: Extend only the preceding stage’s counts; plus and minus are distinct choices even for zero.
Do not deduplicate sign paths that share a total.

permutation-in-string.question: How can a fixed-size letter inventory recognize a rearrangement?
intuition: Generating every permutation of the query is unnecessary. Any rearrangement has exactly the same occurrence count for every letter and exactly the same length.
Slide a section of query length across the text while maintaining its letter counts. Compare its inventory with the query’s inventory. A matching inventory means that section is a permutation.
permutation-in-string.observation: Both letter multiplicities and section length must match.
approach: Count the query’s letters.
Maintain text sections of exactly the query length.
Update leaving and entering counts and test for inventory equality.
permutation-in-string.correctness: Two equal-length strings are permutations exactly when every letter count agrees. The sliding updates remove precisely the leaving character and add precisely the entering one, keeping each section’s inventory exact. Every possible start of a query-length section is checked, so a match is found if and only if one exists.
permutation-in-string.cost: Counting and scanning are linear in the two text lengths. Inventory comparison uses the fixed 26-letter alphabet, so extra storage is constant.
pitfalls: Both letter multiplicities and section length must match.

task-scheduler.question: Why can the most repeated tasks force idle slots?
intuition: Scheduling each task as soon as possible without considering its repeated copies can create avoidable late gaps. The maximum frequency sets a spacing frame that every schedule must satisfy.

Place the most frequent task copies into successive rounds separated by the cooldown. The first rounds require cooldown-plus-one slots, and the final round needs one slot for every task tied at maximum frequency. The answer is the larger of this frame size and the total task count.

approach: Count task frequencies and find the largest count.
Count how many task labels attain that frequency.
Compare the forced spacing frame with total work.
task-scheduler.correctness: Copies of a maximum-frequency task force all but the final copy to occupy distinct cooldown-separated rounds. Tied maximum labels require separate final slots, giving the frame lower bound. Every task also needs a slot. Distributing less frequent tasks through the rounds fills gaps without increasing this bound; if there are more tasks than frame slots, their own count determines the schedule length.
task-scheduler.cost: Count each task once, then inspect the fixed task alphabet. Time is linear in task count and count storage is constant for the 26-letter alphabet.
pitfalls: Cooldown counts intervening slots between two equal tasks.
Do not count cooldown as the full distance between equal tasks; their distance is cooldown plus one.

smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.question: Why must we advance the list currently supplying the minimum?
intuition: Trying every combination of representatives from all lists is enormous. With sorted lists, a current representative from each list gives a complete covering range, and only moving its minimum can raise the lower endpoint.

Keep one current value from every list, compare their minimum, and track their maximum. Record that range, then advance the list that supplied the minimum. Stop when that list has no next value, since further complete frontiers are impossible.
smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.observation: Every candidate frontier includes one representative from each list.
approach: Start at each list’s first value.
Record the minimum-to-maximum frontier range.
Advance the minimum’s list and continue until one list is exhausted.
smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.correctness: For a fixed minimum representative, advancing any other list cannot improve the lower endpoint and cannot lower the maximum. Thus all potentially better ranges arise by advancing the minimum’s list. The process visits those necessary frontiers in order and records their best range. When a list exhausts at the minimum, no larger lower endpoint can still cover that list.
smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.cost: Each advance processes one list entry with a logarithmic operation over the number of lists. Work is total processed entries times that logarithm; the frontier stores one entry per list.
pitfalls: Every candidate frontier includes one representative from each list.
Stop on exhaustion of the minimum’s list, not when any nonminimum representative happens to be last.

intuition: A depth-first running average can accidentally mix depths. Breadth-first exploration provides all nodes at a depth as one complete group.
Freeze the size of the current level before adding its children. Sum exactly those nodes and divide by that frozen count. Children belong to the next level and must not enter the current denominator.

design-search-autocomplete-system.question: How can each typed prefix already know its three best completions?
intuition: Scanning every stored sentence after each keystroke repeats the same prefix comparisons. Prefix paths can store a small ranked shortlist as history counts change.

Store sentences along a letter-path tree. At each prefix node, cache the three sentences with highest historical count, breaking ties alphabetically. A typed character advances one path; finishing a sentence increases its history count and refreshes shortlists along that sentence’s prefixes.
design-search-autocomplete-system.observation: Rank by descending history count, then ascending sentence text.
approach: Build prefix paths and their best-three shortlists from history.
Advance the active prefix for each ordinary typed character.
On the finishing marker, record the completed sentence, update its prefixes, and reset typing.
design-search-autocomplete-system.correctness: Every sentence passes through exactly the nodes representing its prefixes. Maintaining each node’s best three according to the ranking rule gives exactly the best matches for that prefix. Character-by-character traversal reaches the correct node or establishes no match. A completed sentence updates every affected prefix, keeping future cached answers correct.
design-search-autocomplete-system.cost: Typing follows one path edge and returns a bounded shortlist. Recording a completed sentence walks its length and updates bounded rankings. Stored prefix paths and sentence text determine memory use.
pitfalls: Rank by descending history count, then ascending sentence text.
Frequency ties must use alphabetical order, including spaces.

intuition: Adding every length-four section from scratch repeats most of the same additions. Neighboring equal-length sections differ by exactly one leaving value and one entering value.

Keep a section’s exact sum. Slide by subtracting the leaving value and adding the entering value, recording the greatest sum. Because every section has the same positive length, dividing that greatest sum by the common length gives the greatest average.
maximum-average-subarray-i.observation: Initialize from an actual full-length section, even when all values are negative.
approach: Sum the first section of the requested length.
Update its sum by one leaving and one entering value per slide.
Divide the largest measured sum by the fixed length.
maximum-average-subarray-i.correctness: The initial sum is exact. Each slide removes precisely the departing value and adds precisely the new value, so every subsequent sum remains exact. The first section and all slides enumerate every valid fixed-length section. With a common positive denominator, their sums and averages have identical order.
maximum-average-subarray-i.cost: Summing the first section and updating each slide takes linear total time. Only current and best sums and boundaries are retained, giving constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Initialize from an actual full-length section, even when all values are negative.

palindromic-substrings.question: How does expanding from centers count every positional palindrome exactly once?
intuition: Testing every section by reading it backward repeatedly checks the same interior characters. Every palindrome instead has a unique middle character or middle gap.

Start at each character and each gap between characters. Expand outward while the two new endpoints match. Each successful expansion is one positional palindrome, even when its text equals a palindrome elsewhere.
palindromic-substrings.observation: Count positions, not distinct spellings, and include both character and gap centers.
approach: Choose every odd-length and even-length center.
Count each matching expansion before growing outward again.
Stop that center on a mismatch or text boundary.
palindromic-substrings.correctness: Every palindrome has exactly one center and radius. Its mirrored pairs all match, so that center’s expansion reaches and counts it. Conversely, each successful expansion wraps matching endpoints around a valid interior and is palindromic. Unique center-radius pairs ensure no positional substring is counted twice.
palindromic-substrings.cost: There are linearly many centers, each allowing a linear number of expansions in the worst case. Time is quadratic in text length and extra storage is constant.
pitfalls: Count positions, not distinct spellings, and include both character and gap centers.
Ignoring gap centers misses every even-length palindrome.

maximum-binary-tree.question: Why does a larger arriving value become the parent of smaller trailing roots?
intuition: Recursively scanning for the maximum of every subsection can be quadratic. A decreasing stack of pending subtree roots captures the right edge of the tree built so far.

A new value absorbs smaller trailing roots into its left subtree. The last absorbed root already contains the others. If a larger pending ancestor remains, the new node becomes its right child; otherwise it is the new overall root.
maximum-binary-tree.observation: Preserve input inorder order while ensuring each parent is larger than its descendants.
approach: Keep pending roots in decreasing value order.
Pop smaller roots into the new node’s left subtree.
Attach the new node to the remaining larger ancestor’s right side.
maximum-binary-tree.correctness: Before each arrival, pending roots decrease and describe the right boundary of a tree whose inorder sequence is the processed prefix. Absorbing smaller trailing roots keeps them before the new value and below it. Attaching under the remaining larger ancestor preserves both inorder order and maximum-parent ordering, the defining properties of the required unique tree.
maximum-binary-tree.cost: Each node enters the pending stack once and leaves at most once, giving linear work. The pending stack is linear in the worst case, and the returned tree contains one node per input value.
pitfalls: Preserve input inorder order while ensuring each parent is larger than its descendants.
Attach the last popped subtree, which contains earlier popped roots.

find-k-closest-elements.question: How can two neighboring blocks decide which side contains the closest values?
intuition: Sorting every value by distance ignores the input’s order. In a sorted array, the closest requested values can form a continuous block; neighboring blocks differ only at their outer competing values.

Binary search the block’s starting position. Compare the value that would be dropped on the left with the value that would enter on the right, using their directed distances from the target. Keep the left block on ties, because smaller values win.
find-k-closest-elements.observation: A distance tie keeps the smaller left boundary value.
approach: Search all legal starts of a block of the requested size.
Compare the two competing endpoints of neighboring blocks.
Return the chosen block in its existing ascending order.
find-k-closest-elements.correctness: In a sorted sequence, skipping an interior value while retaining farther outer values cannot improve closeness, so an optimal selection is a block. The preference between adjacent blocks changes monotonically as their endpoints move right. Binary search discards only starts whose boundary replacement proves them worse, retaining ties on the smaller-value side.
find-k-closest-elements.cost: Binary search examines logarithmically many block starts; copying the requested block takes time and output space proportional to its size. Auxiliary search storage is constant.
pitfalls: A distance tie keeps the smaller left boundary value.
Use the directed endpoint comparison rather than an unrelated absolute-distance rule.

maximum-width-of-binary-tree.question: Why can three real nodes occupy a level of width four?
intuition: Counting real nodes at a depth misses empty positions between the outside nodes. Creating every missing placeholder can instead explode for a sparse deep tree.

Assign real nodes their conceptual positions in a complete binary tree. At each depth, width is rightmost position minus leftmost position plus one. Translate all positions by the first position at that depth to keep numbers manageable without changing gaps.
maximum-width-of-binary-tree.observation: Measure endpoint spacing, including interior gaps, while queueing only real nodes.
approach: Traverse one depth at a time with conceptual node positions.
Translate the level’s positions by its first coordinate.
Measure its last translated position plus one and record the maximum.
maximum-width-of-binary-tree.correctness: The child-position rule matches complete-tree slots, so positions encode every interior gap. Subtracting a common offset preserves their pairwise differences. Breadth-first order gives the first and last real positions at each depth, whose inclusive span is exactly the requested width.
maximum-width-of-binary-tree.cost: Each real node is visited once. Queue storage depends on the maximum number of real nodes per depth, not on the potentially much larger gap-inclusive width.
pitfalls: Measure endpoint spacing, including interior gaps, while queueing only real nodes.
Queue size measures real nodes and may be much smaller than conceptual width.

number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.question: How can an endpoint remember both its best length and the number of ways to achieve it?
intuition: A single longest-length answer loses how many distinct index selections achieve that length. Each endpoint needs a count alongside its best increasing length.

For every position, consider smaller earlier values as possible predecessors. A strictly better proposed length replaces the count; an equally good length adds another predecessor’s count. Sum counts at all endpoints attaining the global longest length.
number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.observation: Replace counts for longer proposals; add counts only for equally long proposals.
approach: Start each endpoint with its singleton length one and count one.
Extend from every smaller earlier value, tracking best length and its count.
Add counts at all endpoints with maximum length.
number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.correctness: Every increasing subsequence ending at a position is either its singleton or extends a uniquely determined smaller earlier predecessor. Longer proposals supersede shorter ones; tied best proposals have disjoint predecessor identities and their counts add. Induction gives exact best lengths and counts at each endpoint, and the final endpoint sum counts each longest sequence once.
number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.cost: Each endpoint compares against all earlier endpoints, giving quadratic time. Two linear-size tables store lengths and counts.
pitfalls: Replace counts for longer proposals; add counts only for equally long proposals.
Do not add counts from shorter proposals.

partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.question: Why can the set of used positions determine the unfinished group’s total?
intuition: Assigning values to labeled buckets repeatedly explores equivalent group arrangements. Every completed group has the same target sum, so the used-value total determines the current remainder modulo that target.

Represent a state by which input positions have been used and the unfinished group’s sum. Add an unused value only if it fits; completing the target resets the remainder to zero. Distinct positions stay distinct even when values are equal.
partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.observation: Positive values and equal target sums make the used-position state sufficient.
approach: Check divisibility of the total by the group count and reject oversized values.
Begin with no positions used and an empty current group.
Explore fitting unused positions until every position is used in complete target groups.
partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.correctness: A reachable state consists of completed target groups and one unfinished group within capacity. Adding a fitting unused value preserves this structure; reaching the target begins a new empty group. Every valid partition can be built group by group through such states. Positivity prevents empty completed groups, and the full total fixes their count.
partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.cost: There are at most two-to-the-item-count used-position states, each considering every unused position. Time is item count times that exponential bound, and the remainder table has exponential storage.
pitfalls: Positive values and equal target sums make the used-position state sufficient.
Treat equal-valued occurrences as distinct positions, each used once.

subarray-product-less-than-k.question: Why does a valid positive-product section certify all its ending suffixes?
intuition: Multiplying every possible section is quadratic. With all factors at least one, removing factors cannot increase a section’s product.

Expand a section to the right, then remove left factors until its product is strictly below the threshold. Every suffix ending at this right endpoint is also valid, so the section’s length counts all new valid sections at once.
subarray-product-less-than-k.observation: The product comparison is strict; equality requires shrinking.
approach: Return zero immediately for a threshold at most one.
Multiply in each entering factor and divide out leaving factors until valid.
Add the valid section length for this endpoint.
subarray-product-less-than-k.correctness: For each endpoint, shrinking discards exactly the earliest boundaries with invalid products. All remaining suffixes are valid because factors are at least one; all earlier starts are invalid. Thus section length is exactly the number of valid sections ending there. Distinct right endpoints partition all candidate sections, so summing counts gives the total once.
subarray-product-less-than-k.cost: Each factor enters once and leaves at most once. Time is linear and only a product, boundaries, and count are retained.
pitfalls: The product comparison is strict; equality requires shrinking.
The positive-factor assumption is essential.

longest-word-in-dictionary.question: How can a certified shorter prefix prove a longer word is buildable?
intuition: Choosing the longest dictionary word ignores whether every one-letter-at-a-time prefix exists. Check buildability in increasing word length instead.

Begin with the empty prefix certified. A word is buildable if removing its last letter leaves an already certified word. Sort equal lengths alphabetically and keep the first candidate at every new maximum length.
longest-word-in-dictionary.observation: A long word qualifies only through a complete certified prefix chain.
approach: Order words by length, then alphabetically.
Certify a word only when its immediate shorter prefix is certified.
Update the result only when a certified word is strictly longer.
longest-word-in-dictionary.correctness: Inductively, a certified word’s immediate prefix is already buildable and adding its last letter proves the full word buildable. Conversely, every buildable word has a buildable immediate prefix, processed earlier by length. Alphabetical processing and strict-length updates choose the smallest word among maximum-length qualified words.
longest-word-in-dictionary.cost: Sorting words uses comparison work that may inspect their characters; certification also reads each immediate prefix. Stored sorted entries and certified words are references to input words, with a temporary prefix copy bounded by maximum word length.
pitfalls: A long word qualifies only through a complete certified prefix chain.
Do not require only the immediate prefix’s presence without also certifying its own chain.

find-smallest-letter-greater-than-target.question: How do we find the first strictly greater letter and wrap when it is absent?
intuition: A linear scan is unnecessary in sorted letters. The condition “greater than target” changes only once from false to true, and equality belongs to the false side.

Binary search the boundary before the first greater letter. A middle letter at or below the target discards itself and all earlier letters; a greater letter remains a possible first answer. If the boundary is past the end, wrap to the first letter.
find-smallest-letter-greater-than-target.observation: Equality is invalid, and passing the end triggers circular wraparound.
approach: Search the first position whose letter is strictly greater.
Discard all middle letters at or below the target.
Use the first letter when no greater position exists.
find-smallest-letter-greater-than-target.correctness: Sortedness makes all letters at or below the target precede all greater letters. Each comparison preserves the first greater boundary while halving its possible range. Meeting bounds locates that boundary exactly. If it equals the list length, every letter failed, and the specified wrap rule selects the first.
find-smallest-letter-greater-than-target.cost: Each comparison halves the boundary search, giving logarithmic time and constant auxiliary storage.
pitfalls: Equality is invalid, and passing the end triggers circular wraparound.
Do not treat the final equal letter as a match.

prefix-and-suffix-search.question: How can one letter path enforce both a word’s ending and beginning?
intuition: Filtering all words for each prefix-and-suffix query repeats the same comparisons. Build an index whose paths encode both conditions together.

For each word, store every suffix followed by a special separator and then the full word. A query follows its suffix, the separator, and its prefix. Save the greatest matching word index along each path.
prefix-and-suffix-search.observation: The separator fixes the complete suffix boundary; the following letters need only match the beginning of the word.
approach: Insert suffix–separator–word paths for every indexed word.
Record the latest word index at every visited prefix node.
Follow suffix–separator–prefix for a query, or fail at a missing letter.
prefix-and-suffix-search.correctness: A stored combined path reaches a query endpoint exactly when its suffix portion equals the requested full suffix and its full-word portion begins with the requested prefix. Thus traversal matches both conditions simultaneously. Increasing-index insertion leaves the largest matching index at every endpoint, giving the required tie result.
prefix-and-suffix-search.cost: A word of maximum length supplies linearly many suffix paths, each linear in length, making construction and index storage quadratic in that length per word. A query walks only its suffix and prefix lengths.
pitfalls: The separator fixes the complete suffix boundary; the following letters need only match the beginning of the word.
The separator must not be a permitted word letter.

employee-free-time.question: Why is shared free time the gap between merged busy intervals?
intuition: Comparing every employee pair misses the collective condition: everyone is free only where no employee is busy. Combine all busy intervals into one union.
Sort every employee’s busy interval by start. Extend the current busy ending through overlaps. When a new start lies strictly beyond that ending, the gap between them is free for everyone.
employee-free-time.observation: Return finite positive-length gaps inside the combined schedule, excluding unbounded outside time.
approach: Flatten all busy intervals and sort by start.
Extend the current busy union’s ending across overlaps and nesting.
Emit a gap only before a strictly later next busy start.
employee-free-time.correctness: Sorting starts ensures that no future interval can begin before the next unprocessed start. Extending the busy ending captures the union of all overlapping processed intervals. A strict gap before the next start contains no processed or future busy interval, so everyone is free there. Conversely, every finite common free region appears between consecutive union components.
employee-free-time.cost: Flattening and sorting all busy intervals takes linearithmic time and linear extra storage. The union scan is linear, in addition to returned free gaps.
pitfalls: Return finite positive-length gaps inside the combined schedule, excluding unbounded outside time.
A nested interval cannot move the busy ending backward.

reorganize-string.question: How can the previous letter wait outside the available choices?
intuition: Choosing the most common remaining letter repeatedly can create equal neighbors. Conversely, postponing a high-frequency letter too long can leave an impossible final run.

Choose the most frequent currently eligible letter, and hold its remaining copies aside for one step. After placing a different letter, release the preceding held supply. A preliminary count check rejects a letter that cannot be separated by all the others.
reorganize-string.observation: The letter just used cannot be the next available choice.
approach: Count letters and reject a maximum count exceeding half the rounded-up text length.
Select the largest eligible remaining supply.
Hold that letter outside the choices until a different letter is placed.
reorganize-string.correctness: Holding the previous letter guarantees adjacency safety. Choosing the largest eligible remaining demand uses difficult-to-separate copies early; swapping such a choice into a feasible arrangement does not reduce the separator supply for smaller demands. The maximum-count bound is necessary because every repeated copy after the first needs another letter between it and its predecessor, and this greedy construction realizes a valid arrangement when that bound holds.
reorganize-string.cost: Each output character performs logarithmic priority work over distinct letters. Counts and priority entries scale with the alphabet, and the constructed output with text length.
pitfalls: The letter just used cannot be the next available choice.
Do not append the held letter directly when no different letter is available.

binary-search.question: Why can one comparison eliminate half a sorted array?
intuition: A linear search checks values whose relative order already rules them out. In sorted input, comparing a middle value to the target certifies an entire side.

Keep the range where the target could still occur. A middle value below the target excludes itself and everything left; a value above excludes itself and everything right. Equality returns the original position.
binary-search.observation: The remaining range always contains the target if it exists.
approach: Begin with the whole sorted array as candidates.
Compare the middle value and discard the impossible half.
Return its position on equality or absence when the range empties.
binary-search.correctness: Sortedness makes the discarded half incapable of containing the target after each unequal comparison. Thus the candidate-range invariant is preserved. Equality gives a valid position, while an empty range proves that no original position can contain the target.
binary-search.cost: The candidate range at least halves after each unequal comparison. Time is logarithmic and the two boundaries use constant extra storage.
pitfalls: The remaining range always contains the target if it exists.
Exclude the compared unequal midpoint so the range strictly shrinks.

letter-case-permutation.question: Why do digits continue one path while letters split it in two?
intuition: Enumerating all character replacements would change digits and introduce invalid strings. Only alphabetic positions have two permitted choices; digits remain fixed.

Build an output prefix character by character. At a letter, branch into lowercase and uppercase. At a digit, append it unchanged on the same path. Each complete path chooses one case for every letter.
letter-case-permutation.observation: Only letters branch; every character retains its original position.
approach: Advance through the input positions in order.
Choose both cases for each letter and one unchanged choice for a digit.
Record each completed text and undo choices to explore the other paths.
letter-case-permutation.correctness: Every branch changes only the current letter to one of its two allowed cases or preserves the current digit. A complete path is therefore valid. Every legal case assignment chooses exactly one branch at each letter, so the search includes all possibilities without duplication.
letter-case-permutation.cost: There are two-to-the-letter-count outputs, each requiring the full text length to write. The working prefix and recursion depth are linear in text length, besides the exponential output.
pitfalls: Only letters branch; every character retains its original position.
Count branching letters, not total text length, when counting results.

count-unique-characters-of-all-substring.question: How many sections contain one occurrence but exclude its equal-letter neighbors?
intuition: Listing every section and counting its unique letters repeats enormous work. Instead, let each occurrence contribute to precisely the sections in which it is the only copy of its letter.

For an occurrence, its previous equal letter limits the left boundary and its next equal letter limits the right boundary. The number of valid sections is the number of left choices times the number of right choices. Finalize an occurrence when its next equal letter is discovered.
count-unique-characters-of-all-substring.observation: An occurrence is unique only between its neighboring equal-letter positions.
approach: Track the two latest positions of each letter.
When another copy appears, finalize the preceding copy’s boundary-choice product.
Use the text’s end boundary to finalize each last occurrence.
count-unique-characters-of-all-substring.correctness: A section makes an occurrence unique exactly when it includes that position, starts after the previous equal letter, and ends before the next equal letter. Left and right boundaries are independent, so their choice counts multiply. Every unique letter in every section belongs to exactly one such occurrence, making the contribution sum exact.
count-unique-characters-of-all-substring.cost: Each character finalizes a previous occurrence once, followed by one finalization per distinct letter. Time is linear and remembered positions scale with the fixed uppercase alphabet.
pitfalls: An occurrence is unique only between its neighboring equal-letter positions.
Include the outside boundaries before the first and after the last position.

backspace-string-compare.question: How can reading backward skip deleted letters without rebuilding editor contents?
intuition: Constructing both edited texts works but stores extra strings. Reading from the end lets each backspace announce how many earlier ordinary characters must be skipped.

Move backward with a pending-deletion count. A backspace adds one deletion; an ordinary character consumes one if pending, otherwise survives. Compare the next surviving character from each text and repeat.
backspace-string-compare.observation: Backspaces delete earlier characters, so reverse reading accumulates deletion demand.
approach: Find each text’s next surviving character from the right.
Compare survivors, rejecting a mismatch or one-sided exhaustion.
Continue until both texts have no survivor left.
backspace-string-compare.correctness: Reverse scanning accounts for exactly the backspaces to the right of each character. Pending deletions consume precisely the ordinary characters those backspaces erase; the next uncovered character is therefore the next edited survivor from the end. Comparing every survivor and simultaneous exhaustion is equivalent to comparing the two edited texts.
backspace-string-compare.cost: Both scans move only backward and visit each character a constant number of times. Work is linear in combined text length and deletion counters use constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Backspaces delete earlier characters, so reverse reading accumulates deletion demand.
A backspace encountered while deletions are pending adds another deletion.

peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.question: Which side of a sloping middle edge must contain the summit?
intuition: A full scan finds the maximum but ignores the promised rise-then-fall structure. One adjacent comparison reveals whether the middle lies before or at/after the summit.

Compare a middle entry with its next entry. An upward edge places the summit strictly to the right. A downward edge places it at the middle or to the left. Keep that possible summit range until one position remains.
peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.observation: An upward edge discards the middle; a downward edge keeps it as a possible summit.
approach: Begin with the entire mountain range.
Compare the middle value with the next value.
Keep the side containing the summit until the boundaries meet.
peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.correctness: In a strict mountain, every edge before the peak rises and every edge after it falls. The adjacent comparison therefore determines which retained side includes the unique peak. Each update preserves that peak and shrinks the range, so the final position is exactly its index.
peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.cost: The candidate interval halves on each comparison. Time is logarithmic and the boundaries use constant extra storage.
pitfalls: An upward edge discards the middle; a downward edge keeps it as a possible summit.
Keep a falling midpoint instead of discarding a possible summit.

all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.question: How does a target-centered wave travel through parents as well as children?
intuition: A search confined to the target’s descendants misses nearby nodes reached through its parent. Treat each tree link as traversable in both directions.

First record each node’s parent. Start a breadth-first wave at the target, using left child, right child, and parent as neighbors. Mark visited nodes to avoid immediately returning along the same link, and stop expanding at the requested distance.
all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.observation: Distance counts edges from the target, regardless of the original root direction.
approach: Build parent links while locating the target.
Explore outward in distance layers through all three possible neighbors.
Return the layer at the requested distance without expanding it.
all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.correctness: Parent links convert the tree into its undirected neighbor relation. Breadth-first exploration discovers a node through the fewest edges from the target, and each next wave is exactly one edge farther. Visited marking prevents duplicates. Thus the requested wave contains every and only the nodes at that distance.
all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.cost: Parent construction visits every node once, and the distance search visits each reached node once. Time and auxiliary maps, queues, and seen records are linear in tree size.
pitfalls: Distance counts edges from the target, regardless of the original root direction.

middle-of-the-linked-list.question: Why does one traveler reach the middle when another runs off the end?
intuition: Counting the full list and restarting works, but two travelers can determine the midpoint in one pass. One advances one link per round, the other two.

Begin both at the head. Advance the slower traveler once whenever the faster can advance twice. When the fast traveler reaches the end or last node, the slow traveler is at the middle; for even length it lands on the required second middle.
middle-of-the-linked-list.observation: Advance while the fast traveler and its next node both exist.
approach: Place both travelers at the first node.
Move slow by one and fast by two links each round.
Return the original node where slow stops.
middle-of-the-linked-list.correctness: After each round, slow has advanced one link for every two fast links. For length 2m, fast exits after m rounds and slow occupies position m, the second middle. For length 2m+1, fast reaches the last node after m rounds and slow occupies position m, the sole middle.

pitfalls: Advance while the fast traveler and its next node both exist.
Return the original middle node, rather than a copied list of its values.

maximum-frequency-stack.question: How can frequency levels remember the most recent tied occurrence?
intuition: A normal stack knows recency but not which value is most frequent. Recounting all pushes at every removal is unnecessary if each frequency increase records its own recency.

Count each value’s active occurrences. When a push raises its frequency to a level, append it to that level’s stack. Pop from the highest nonempty level; its most recent entry resolves frequency ties. Lower-level records remain ready for later removals.
maximum-frequency-stack.observation: Priority is maximum active frequency, then most recent unmatched push.
approach: Track each value’s active frequency and a recency stack for every level.
Push the value into the stack of its new frequency.
Pop the latest entry at the maximum level and lower that level when empty.
maximum-frequency-stack.correctness: A value reaching frequency f records the unmatched push that made its fth active occurrence. Higher levels take priority, so that event remains until the value returns to frequency f. Among all maximum-frequency values, the newest such event is their newest unmatched push. Popping its level stack therefore implements both the frequency and recency rules.
maximum-frequency-stack.cost: Frequency updates and level-stack pushes and pops are constant amortized work. One record per active push gives storage proportional to active occurrences.
pitfalls: Priority is maximum active frequency, then most recent unmatched push.
Do not erase lower-level history when a frequency increases.

fruit-into-baskets.question: Why does a third fruit type force the starting tree to move?
intuition: Trying every starting tree independently repeats long harvests. The two baskets allow unlimited quantities but only two distinct types within one continuous run.
Maintain a section and counts of its fruit types. Add the next tree, then remove left trees until at most two types remain. Record the largest valid section length.
fruit-into-baskets.observation: Basket capacity limits distinct types, not total fruit count.
approach: Count types in the current continuous section.
Expand right, shrinking left only when a third type appears.
Remember the longest section containing at most two types.
fruit-into-baskets.correctness: For each right endpoint, shrinking removes only starts whose section still has more than two types. Removing left values cannot add a type, so the first retained start gives the longest valid section ending there. A discarded start cannot regain validity by adding later trees. Maximizing those endpoint results finds the best continuous harvest.
fruit-into-baskets.cost: Every tree enters and leaves the section at most once. The count map holds at most three types during adjustment, giving linear time and constant extra storage.
pitfalls: Basket capacity limits distinct types, not total fruit count.
Do not shrink merely because a type appears more than once.

k-closest-points-to-origin.question: Why can the farthest retained point guard a small collection of nearest points?
intuition: Sorting every point uses more work than needed when only a small count is requested. Keep just that many best candidates and expose the worst one among them.

Compare squared distances, avoiding square roots because squaring preserves nonnegative distance order. Retain up to the requested count in a priority structure with the farthest retained point exposed. Replace that point only when a closer candidate arrives.
k-closest-points-to-origin.observation: The exposed boundary is the farthest retained candidate, not the nearest.
approach: Compute each point’s squared distance from the origin.
Fill the retained collection to its requested size.
Replace its farthest point whenever a strictly closer point arrives.
k-closest-points-to-origin.correctness: Before the collection fills, every seen point is retained. Once full, it contains the closest requested number among seen points: a new farther point cannot improve it, while a closer point must replace its farthest member. Induction preserves this best-candidate set through the entire scan.
k-closest-points-to-origin.cost: Each point performs at most one logarithmic operation over the retained count. Time is input size times that logarithm, and retained entries and output use requested-count storage.
pitfalls: The exposed boundary is the farthest retained candidate, not the nearest.
Do not prioritize a point by one coordinate alone.

squares-of-a-sorted-array.question: Why must the largest remaining square come from an endpoint?
intuition: Squaring an ascending array does not preserve order across negative values. Sorting the squares works, but the largest magnitude among remaining sorted values is always at one of the two ends.
Compare endpoint squares, place the larger at the last unfilled output position, and move only that endpoint inward. Fill from largest to smallest so the final output is ascending.
squares-of-a-sorted-array.observation: Fill the output backward while consuming one original occurrence per step.
approach: Compare squares at the current left and right endpoints.
Write the larger into the last open output position.
Move that endpoint inward and continue.
squares-of-a-sorted-array.correctness: For a sorted remaining interval, no interior value has greater absolute magnitude than both endpoints. The larger endpoint square is therefore the greatest remaining output value. Placing it at the last open position preserves a correctly sorted suffix; induction completes all squares in ascending order.
squares-of-a-sorted-array.cost: Each endpoint occurrence is consumed once, giving linear time. The output has one entry per input value; auxiliary boundaries require constant storage.
pitfalls: Fill the output backward while consuming one original occurrence per step.
Do not assume the squared input is already sorted.

interval-list-intersections.question: Why does the interval ending first have no future overlap left to explore?
intuition: Comparing every pair of intervals ignores that each list is sorted and internally disjoint. Only the currently earliest remaining interval from each list can overlap next.

Their common range starts at the larger start and ends at the smaller end. Record it when those boundaries do not cross. Then advance the interval ending first, since later intervals in the other list cannot overlap it.

approach: Compare the current interval of each list.
Record the larger-start to smaller-end range if nonempty.
Advance the interval with the earlier end.
interval-list-intersections.correctness: The larger start and smaller end are exactly the common bounds of a pair. Once one current interval ends before the other, it cannot meet any later interval in the other internally disjoint sorted list. Advancing it therefore discards no possible intersection. Repeating checks all potentially overlapping pairs and records each once.
interval-list-intersections.cost: Every comparison advances at least one list position, giving time linear in the combined interval count. Only current positions are auxiliary storage, besides the intersection output.
pitfalls: Closed endpoints permit a one-point intersection when the boundaries are equal.

index-pairs-of-a-string.question: How can a shared word-prefix tree recognize overlapping text matches?
intuition: Searching separately for every dictionary word repeats comparisons along shared beginnings. A letter-path tree combines those beginnings and allows one forward walk from each text start.

From every start position, follow text letters through dictionary prefix paths. Record a pair each time a complete-word endpoint is reached, but continue because a longer word may also match. Stop only when the path is absent.
index-pairs-of-a-string.observation: Matches may overlap and use inclusive end positions.
approach: Build a letter-path tree with complete-word markers.
Start one forward path walk at each text position.
Record every endpoint encountered, continuing for longer matches.
index-pairs-of-a-string.correctness: A path from a text start exists exactly while the scanned text is a prefix of some dictionary word. An endpoint marks exact equality with a whole word, so each recorded pair is valid. Every occurrence has a start scanned by the algorithm and a complete path to its end. Increasing starts and increasing ends within each walk supply the requested order.
index-pairs-of-a-string.cost: Dictionary construction reads all word characters. Each text start walks at most the smaller of remaining text length and maximum word length. Prefix-tree storage scales with dictionary characters, excluding result pairs.
pitfalls: Matches may overlap and use inclusive end positions.
Do not stop at the first complete word if longer paths remain.

convert-1d-array-into-2d-array.question: How does row-major position determine a cell without changing value order?
intuition: A reshape should preserve the sequence, not rearrange it. The requested rectangle must contain exactly as many cells as the original array has entries.

Check rows times columns against input length. If equal, divide the original sequence into consecutive blocks of column-count length, one block per row. Each original position belongs to one exact row and column.
convert-1d-array-into-2d-array.observation: Reject a shape whose cell count differs from the original entry count.
approach: Verify the requested rectangle has the exact number of entries.
Read one consecutive column-width block for each row.
Return those rows in the original sequence order.
convert-1d-array-into-2d-array.correctness: For a valid shape, consecutive equal-width blocks partition every original position once. Row order and within-row order match the original sequence, so every value reaches its required row-major cell. If cell count differs, preserving all entries exactly once is impossible and rejection is correct.
convert-1d-array-into-2d-array.cost: An invalid shape is rejected in constant time. A valid reshape copies each entry once, taking time and output storage proportional to cell count, with constant auxiliary bookkeeping.
pitfalls: Reject a shape whose cell count differs from the original entry count.
Do not pad missing entries or silently discard extras.

valid-anagram.question: How can consuming a letter inventory prove two texts are rearrangements?
intuition: Equal sets of letters are insufficient because occurrence counts matter. An anagram must use every copy of each letter exactly once.

Require equal lengths, count the first text’s letters, then consume one count per letter in the second text. Any demand beyond available supply rejects the match; equal length ensures no unused supply remains if no deficit occurs.
valid-anagram.observation: Compare multiplicities, not letter membership or original order.
approach: Reject unequal lengths.
Count letter occurrences in the first text.
Consume the second text’s letters, rejecting a negative remaining count.
valid-anagram.correctness: Counting records exactly the first text’s multiset of letters. Every consumed second-text letter removes one required copy; a negative count proves a missing copy. If lengths agree and no count becomes negative, the same total number of copies was consumed, so all counts end at zero and the multisets are equal.
valid-anagram.cost: Each character is counted or consumed once. Time is linear in combined lengths and the lowercase alphabet’s 26 counts use constant storage.
pitfalls: Compare multiplicities, not letter membership or original order.
Keep separate counts for repeated copies.
valid-anagram.artAlt: Require equal lengths, count the first text’s letters, then consume one count per letter in the second text. Any demand beyond available supply rejects the match; equal length ensures no unused supply remains if no deficit occurs.

Append the word and return all completed groups.

Appending once per original occurrence preserves the input’s full multiplicity, producing precisely its anagram equivalence classes.

pitfalls: Equal inventories imply the same group; every input occurrence remains in the output.

encode-and-decode-strings.question: Why can a length header preserve text containing every possible separator?
intuition: Joining texts with a separator fails when a payload contains that separator. An empty text also needs an explicit record so it cannot disappear between boundaries.

Write each text’s decimal character length, a header delimiter, and its exact payload. During decoding, read the delimiter only to end the numeric header, then consume precisely the announced character count. Payload delimiters are ordinary data.
encode-and-decode-strings.observation: Only headers search for delimiters; payloads are read by their declared lengths.
approach: Encode each record as length, header delimiter, and payload.
Join the records into one stream.
Decode a numeric header, consume that many characters, and repeat.
encode-and-decode-strings.correctness: Every header announces the exact following payload length, so the receiver identifies its endpoint regardless of payload characters. Starting the next header at that endpoint preserves record alignment. Inductively all original records are recovered in order, including a zero-length record represented by an explicit zero header.
encode-and-decode-strings.cost: Encoding and decoding read the payload and headers once. Work and stored stream/output scale with total payload characters plus record count.
pitfalls: Only headers search for delimiters; payloads are read by their declared lengths.
The format assumes a well-formed stream from the encoder.

intuition: Comparing the raw text includes characters the problem excludes. Constructing a cleaned copy works, but two inward-moving scans can skip irrelevant characters directly.

At both ends, skip nonletters and nondigits. Compare the next meaningful characters without case differences, then move inward. A mismatch rejects immediately; meeting or crossing means all meaningful mirrored pairs agree.
valid-palindrome.observation: Letters and digits participate; punctuation and spaces do not.
approach: Move both ends past irrelevant characters.
Compare the meaningful pair in a common case.
Continue inward until mismatch or all pairs have matched.
valid-palindrome.correctness: Skipping nonalphanumeric characters exposes the next outermost pair of the normalized sequence. If those characters differ after case normalization, the sequence cannot be palindromic. If they match, removing the pair preserves the same question for its interior. Meeting bounds proves every mirrored pair matches.
valid-palindrome.cost: Each scan crosses every original position at most once. Time is linear and only two positions and temporary characters use auxiliary storage.
pitfalls: Letters and digits participate; punctuation and spaces do not.
Do not skip a digit merely because it is not a letter.

valid-parentheses.question: Why must a closing bracket match the most recent unmatched opening?
intuition: Equal counts of opening and closing brackets do not ensure valid nesting or type. The innermost unfinished pair must close before any outer pair can close.

Keep unmatched openings in a last-in-first-out stack. An opening adds its type. A closing must find its matching type at the top, then removes it. Acceptance also requires no unmatched openings at the end.
valid-parentheses.observation: Only the newest unmatched opener is eligible to close.
approach: Push each opening bracket.
For a closing bracket, require a matching top opener and remove it.
Accept only if the stack is empty after the entire text.
valid-parentheses.correctness: The stack always contains exactly the unmatched openings of the processed prefix in nesting order. A valid closer must complete the newest one, so matching and popping preserves that invariant. Any failed match cannot be repaired later. An empty stack at successful exhaustion proves all pairs closed in the proper order and type.
valid-parentheses.cost: Each bracket is processed once and each opener is pushed and removed at most once. Time is linear; all-open input gives linear stack storage.
pitfalls: Only the newest unmatched opener is eligible to close.
Do not search deeper in the stack for a matching opener.

design-add-and-search-words-data-structu.question: How can a wildcard keep several possible word paths alive?
intuition: A plain word lookup cannot represent a period that matches any one letter. Enumerating all alphabet replacements can waste work on prefixes no stored word has.

Store complete words in a letter-path tree. A literal advances each possible path along its matching edge; a period follows all available letter edges. After the query ends, accept only a path marked as a complete word.
design-add-and-search-words-data-structu.observation: A period consumes exactly one letter, and a matching prefix alone is not a complete-word match.
approach: Insert words into shared letter paths and mark their endpoints.
Keep all path nodes matching the query prefix so far.
Advance literals or wildcard branches, then require a complete endpoint.
design-add-and-search-words-data-structu.correctness: After each consumed query character, the frontier contains exactly the stored prefixes matching that query prefix: literal transitions preserve only the specified letter, and wildcard transitions include every one-letter continuation. Induction establishes exact prefix matching. Requiring an endpoint after the last character then gives exactly whole-word matches.
design-add-and-search-words-data-structu.cost: Insertion follows the word length. A query may branch by every wildcard, with the alphabet and wildcard count bounding the frontier. Stored shared prefixes and the active search frontier determine storage.
pitfalls: A period consumes exactly one letter, and a matching prefix alone is not a complete-word match.
Do not traverse a word-end marker as a wildcard letter.

clone-graph.question: How can one remembered copy preserve both cycles and shared neighbors?
intuition: Recursively copying every encountered neighbor without memory loops forever on cycles and creates multiple copies of shared nodes. Node identity must be remembered before its edges are explored.

Map each original node to exactly one new node. Create and record a new copy at first discovery, then reproduce every original adjacency using those mapped copies. All links in the result connect new nodes, while shared originals remain shared copies.
clone-graph.observation: Record a copy before exploring its neighbors.
approach: Create the start node’s copy and remember its original-to-copy mapping.
Process each discovered original node’s connections.
Create unseen neighbor copies once, then link to their mapped copies.
clone-graph.correctness: First-discovery mapping creates one unique clone per reachable original and prevents cyclic rediscovery. Processing every original adjacency creates exactly its corresponding clone adjacency, always between mapped new nodes. Thus node identities are distinct from originals while all cycles and shared-neighbor relationships are preserved.
clone-graph.cost: Each reachable node is discovered once and every adjacency entry copied once. Work is vertices plus edges; the map and queue are vertex-sized and the returned clone also stores all copied edges.
pitfalls: Record a copy before exploring its neighbors.
Do not map solely by value when node identities can differ.

number-of-1-bits.question: Why does removing the lowest one count bits directly?
intuition: Reading every binary position works, but a number with few one bits can be processed one one at a time. Subtracting one reveals a useful boundary change at the lowest set bit.

Subtracting one turns the lowest one into zero and lower trailing zeros into ones. Keeping only positions that were one in both the original and that predecessor removes exactly the original lowest one. Repeat and count removals.
number-of-1-bits.observation: Each step must clear exactly one original one bit.
approach: Find the predecessor of the current positive word.
Keep positions that are one in both words.
Count one removal and repeat until no one bits remain.
number-of-1-bits.correctness: The predecessor changes precisely the lowest one and all lower zeros. Intersecting one positions with the original clears that lowest one, retains every higher one, and excludes all newly created lower ones. Each iteration reduces the number of original ones by exactly one, so the number of iterations is the desired count.
number-of-1-bits.cost: Work is proportional to the number of one bits, bounded by the fixed word width. Current word and count use constant storage.
pitfalls: Each step must clear exactly one original one bit.
Count ones, not the number of written binary digits.

reverse-bits.question: Why must zero bits still take their turns in a fixed-width reversal?
intuition: Reversing only until the remaining numeric value becomes zero drops original leading zeros, which must become trailing zeros. The problem reverses exactly 32 positions.

Read one bit from the low end, shift the developing output left to make room, and append that bit. Repeat for all 32 input positions. The earliest extracted low bit is pushed toward the final high end by every later append.
reverse-bits.observation: Process the full fixed width, including every zero position.
approach: Begin with an empty numeric output.
Extract the current low bit and append it to the growing output.
Advance through exactly 32 positions, then return the unsigned result.
reverse-bits.correctness: After each append, the output records the consumed low-end input bits in their extraction order. A later append shifts all earlier extracted bits one place toward the high end. After exactly 32 appends, each original position has moved to its mirror position across the fixed word, yielding the complete reversal.
reverse-bits.cost: Exactly 32 constant-size iterations use a few fixed-width words. Both time and auxiliary storage are constant under the stated width.
pitfalls: Process the full fixed width, including every zero position.
Do not stop when the remaining input value first becomes zero.

sum-of-two-integers.question: How can carry-free bits and shifted carries recombine into the same sum?
intuition: Binary addition has two effects at each position: the output bit without incoming carry, and a carry when both inputs contain one. Separate them and repeat until no carry remains.

Differing bits produce the carry-free word. Positions with two ones generate a carry into the next higher position. Recombine those two words the same way until the carry word is zero, using a fixed 32-bit width for signed values.
sum-of-two-integers.observation: Every round preserves the total modulo the fixed width while moving carries upward.
approach: Represent both inputs as fixed-width binary words.
Form differing-bit output and shifted common-one carries.
Repeat until no carries remain, then interpret the signed result.
sum-of-two-integers.correctness: At every bit, a single one contributes that bit’s value, while two ones contribute one carry at twice that value. Thus the carry-free word and shifted carry preserve the combined sum modulo the fixed word width. Carries move left each round and eventually disappear. Interpreting the final word with the specified signed representation yields the ordinary in-range integer sum.
sum-of-two-integers.cost: Carries can travel through at most 32 positions. This fixed bound makes time and storage constant.

longest-common-subsequence.question: How do matching endpoints extend earlier agreement while mismatches preserve it?
intuition: Trying all subsequences is exponential. Every pair of text prefixes has a smaller agreement question whose answer can be saved.

If the two final prefix letters agree, extend the shorter-prefix diagonal answer by one. Otherwise, skip either final letter and retain the better neighboring answer. Keep only the preceding and current rows because older rows are no longer needed.

Induction over prefix pairs establishes every table entry and the complete-text result.

rotate-array.question: Why do three reversals move the final block forward without reversing its final order?
intuition: Shifting one position repeatedly takes too much work for large rotation counts. A right rotation swaps two blocks while preserving the order inside each.

Call the prefix block A and the final requested-count block B. Reversing the whole array gives reversed B followed by reversed A. Reversing those two segments separately restores each block’s internal order, leaving B followed by A.
rotate-array.observation: Reduce the rotation count by full array-length revolutions before splitting the blocks.
approach: Reduce the requested right shift modulo array length.
Reverse the entire array.
Reverse the moved front block and the remaining back block separately.
rotate-array.correctness: Every nontrivial rotation splits the sequence into A followed by B, with desired result B followed by A. Reversing the whole sequence yields reversed B followed by reversed A. Reversing each segment is its own inverse, so the next two reversals yield exactly B followed by A, preserving every original occurrence.
rotate-array.cost: The three reversals swap only a linear number of pairs in the original array. Time is linear and the endpoint references and swaps use constant auxiliary storage.
pitfalls: Reduce the rotation count by full array-length revolutions before splitting the blocks.
Apply the right-rotation split after reducing the count.
